faqs.a: Brussels is negotiating a reform, the so-called digital omnibus, that could change which measurement cookies need permission. The Commission proposed it in November 2025 and the European Parliament and the Council are still working on it. It is not law, it has no adoption date and nobody knows what the final text will say. Until then, what applies is the LSSI and the AEPD guide.

kit-digital-web.intro: When the twelve months of Kit Digital maintenance end, your website stays online, but the domain, the hosting and the updates become your responsibility. Start by finding out what you have. Check that the domain is in your name, ask for every login and a full backup, and then decide whether to keep, move or rebuild it.

seccions.titol: What happens to the website when the maintenance ends?
seccions.text:
The Kit Digital rules (Orden ETD/1498/2021) spell it out. Article 22 sets two phases. A first one of up to three months and a second one of twelve months, counted from the invoice date. Article 18 sets twelve months of service for the website solution, and article 13 requires incident support with a resolution time of under 24 hours. Once those twelve months are up, the service the grant paid for ends.
On its programme page, Red.es lists October 2025 as the end date and more than 900,000 grants awarded. If your invoice dates from late 2025 or early 2026, the twelve months run out between late 2026 and early 2027. Find it and note the date.

seccions.titol: Who owns the domain, and who owns the website?
seccions.text:
The domain must be yours. Annex IV of the rules states that ownership of the domain belongs entirely to the business (“la titularidad del dominio será en su totalidad de la pyme”). Check the registrar's panel or ask the agent in whose name it is registered. If it is in their name, ask for the transfer now.
Ask the same about hosting. Annex IV only required a minimum of twelve months of hosting, and it may sit in your account or in the agent's. Ask whose name it is in, when it expires and what renewal costs. If it is not yours, the site will need to move before that account closes.

seccions.titol: Which logins and backups should you ask for?
seccions.text:
Ask for everything in writing before the service ends. Annex IV of the rules required a content management platform so you could edit the website without the provider's help. An editor account is not enough. You need an administrator account, which in WordPress gives access to every administration feature, plus a recovery email that belongs to you.
WordPress.org puts it plainly. A backup has two parts, the database and the files, and you need both to restore the site. Keep copies in more than one place and make a fresh one before every update.

seccions.titol: Keep it, move it or rebuild it?
seccions.text:
It depends on how the site performs and who can look after it. If it brings enquiries, is easy to edit and everything is in your name, keep it. If the hosting or the licences depend on the agent, move it to your own accounts first. Rebuild only if it fails to explain the business or cannot be edited.
If you have to move it, do so while the old site is still live. Copy the files and the database, set it up on the new hosting, test it and change the DNS last. Keep the old copy in case you need it.

seccions.titol: What should you check before paying for more?
seccions.text:
Before you pay for maintenance or a move, look at the real state of the website. Annex IV of the rules required a site that works on every device, level AA accessibility (WCAG 2.1), at least three pages or sections and basic SEO on two of them. Check whether yours meets that, because it is the starting point.
WordPress.org recommends always running the latest version and backing up before you update. Minor and security updates install themselves, but major releases, the theme and the plugins need someone to review them. If nobody does, the site falls behind and every change costs more.

seccions.titol: What should you ask for before deciding?
seccions.text:
Ask for proposals you can compare. Whether you renew with the agent or look for a studio in Girona, ask in writing what maintenance covers (updates, backups, security and changes), whose name each account will be in and what happens if you leave.
If you decide to rebuild, explain what the new website has to achieve and what you want to keep, such as the domain, the addresses that already rank and the content that works. Our guide on website quotations lists what to compare.

seccions.titol: How we review it from Caldes de Malavella
seccions.text: At crida studio we start by looking at what you have. Domain, hosting, logins, backups and the state of WordPress. We explain it in plain language. We work with small businesses across Girona, the Costa Brava and the rest of Catalonia. If the website works, we will tell you to keep it. If it needs moving or rebuilding, we prepare a proposal with the scope, the responsibilities and what stays in your name.

faqs.q: Does a Kit Digital website go offline when the maintenance ends?
faqs.a: Not by itself. It stays online as long as the domain and the hosting are paid for. What ends is the agent's service, including support and updates. If the domain or the hosting expire and nobody renews them, the site goes down. So find out who holds each contract and when it runs out.

faqs.q: Can I change provider once the Kit Digital service is over?
faqs.a: Yes. Annex IV of the rules required the domain to be in your name and a content management platform so you could edit the site without the provider. Once the second phase ends, you can hire maintenance from anyone, move the site to your own hosting or commission a new one.

faqs.q: What if the domain is registered in the agent's name?
faqs.a: Ask for the transfer now. Annex IV of the Kit Digital rules says the domain must belong to the business. If the agent registered it under their own account, they can transfer it or change the registrant. Keep the confirmation, because without the domain you lose both the website and your email.

mode-ia-google.intro: You can now see it in Search Console. Since 31 August 2026, Google has opened to every website a report showing how often its pages appeared in AI Overviews and AI Mode. It only gives impressions, with no clicks or queries, so it is worth running a manual test every month as well.

seccions.titol: Can Google cite this page in AI Mode?
seccions.text:
Paste the address of a page and the checker reads it once, as Googlebot sees it without JavaScript. According to Google, a page needs to be indexed and allowed to show a snippet to appear as a link in AI Mode and AI Overviews, with no other technical requirement. The eight checks look at exactly that.
It can't tell you whether the page appears for a given question. Google offers no way to check that, which is why the Search Console report and the manual test come further down.

seccions.titol: Where can you see if your site appears in AI Mode?
seccions.text:
In Search Console, among the performance reports, you will find the Generative AI performance report (Search). It shows your site's impressions in AI Overviews and AI Mode. Google introduced it on 3 June 2026 and, as of 31 August 2026, has rolled it out to all websites worldwide.
If you cannot find it, Google's help page says this is usually because the site has not yet received enough impressions in these features, or because you have excluded it with the control described below. In the meantime, check the standard performance report, which already includes this data.

seccions.titol: What does this report count, and what does it leave out?
seccions.text:
It counts impressions. Google defines them as how many times links to your site were shown to a user in a generative AI feature on Google Search. You can break them down by page, country, date and device.
Impressions are the only metric. There are no clicks and no queries, and it does not split AI Overviews from AI Mode. You will know which pages appeared and how often, but not for which question or whether anyone visited your site.

seccions.titol: Is there an AI Mode checker tool?
seccions.text:
Not from Google. No official tool tells you, question by question, whether your site appears in AI Mode. The closest thing is the Generative AI performance report in Search Console, which counts impressions but doesn't show the queries or separate AI Mode from AI Overviews.
Some third-party tools ask AI Mode questions and record which sites it cites. Treat them as a sample, because the answer can change from one person to another and from one day to the next. The ten-question test below does the same by hand, for free. Our checker at the top of this page does something different. It tells you whether anything stops Google from citing a page at all.

seccions.titol: How to run a manual test with ten questions
seccions.text:
Because the report does not tell you which questions brought up your site, test it yourself. Write ten questions the way a customer in Girona would ask when looking for someone to hire, in the languages your customers use, usually Catalan and Spanish, and ask them in AI Mode while signed out.
AI Mode is available in Spain and supports Catalan, Spanish and English, according to Google's help page. Run each question in regular Search too, to see whether an AI Overview appears. Note the date, whether your site is cited, which sources appear and with what wording. Repeat it every month.

seccions.titol: Which sources does AI Mode cite for services in Girona?
seccions.text:
On 30 October 2026 we asked AI Mode 30 unbranded questions, in Catalan, Spanish and English, about services businesses hire in Girona. Websites, branding, SEO, renders, video and automation. It is a small, one-day sample, but it shows what kind of sources get cited.
When the question named a place, it cited service pages that mentioned the town or county, Google Business Profiles, business directories run by public bodies and trade associations, and recently dated articles on the exact topic. For some questions it cited no company at all.

seccions.titol: Should you opt out of AI Mode?
seccions.text:
For most small businesses, no. If you want to be found, opting out means giving up any impressions and clicks that come from AI Overviews and AI Mode, and Google says the control does not change your ranking elsewhere in Search. It only makes sense if your business depends on content you do not want summarised.
The control lives in Search Console under Settings and is called Search generative AI. It has three options. Include, which is the default, exclude, and inherit the setting from the parent property. If you exclude your site, the change usually takes effect within one or two days and the report stops showing data.

seccions.titol: What should you fix first so AI Mode cites you?
seccions.text:
Google says there are no additional requirements and no special optimisations needed to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode. A page has to be indexed and eligible to be shown in Search with a snippet. So the first job is the usual one. Pages that can be read, and that explain clearly what you do and where.
The test sets the order we would follow on a small site in Girona. None of these tasks requires rebuilding the website. Our guide on reviewing whether your company can be found and understood covers each layer and is the natural next step.

faqs.q: Can I see which questions brought my site up in AI Mode?
faqs.a: Not yet. The report shows pages, countries, dates and devices, but not queries. Google says it is looking at adding more metrics over time. Until then, a manual test with real questions is the only way to see which questions bring you up and which sources are cited alongside you.

faqs.q: How can I check if my website is set up correctly for Google AI Mode?
faqs.a: Paste the page address into our free checker at the top of this guide. It looks at the eight things that can stop Google citing the page, such as a noindex tag, a robots.txt block, nosnippet or text that only loads with JavaScript. Google asks for nothing more technical. Then check Search Console to see whether you already appear.

faqs.q: If I cannot see the report in Search Console, does that mean I do not appear?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. According to Google's help page, the report may not appear if the site has not received enough impressions in these features, and it shows no data if you have excluded the site. These impressions are also counted in the standard performance report under the Web search type, so check pages and queries there.

faqs.q: If I exclude my site from generative AI, will my Google rankings drop?
faqs.a: Google says the control is not used as a ranking or inclusion signal affecting other parts of Search. What you lose are the impressions and clicks from AI Overviews and AI Mode. It does not affect AI training either. For that, Google points to Google-Extended.

faqs.q: Does AI Mode work in Catalan?
faqs.a: Yes. Google's help page for AI Mode lists Catalan among the supported languages and Spain among the supported countries. That is why it is worth testing in both Catalan and Spanish. A customer in Girona may ask in either language, and the sources cited can change from one to the other.

render-home-staging-ia.intro: If the home does not exist yet, the most reliable picture is a 3D render built from the plans. If it exists and stands empty, virtual staging helps buyers picture it furnished, as long as you say the furniture is not there. An AI-generated image is useful for testing ideas, and if you publish it and it could pass for real, the EU AI Act asks you to disclose that it was artificially generated or manipulated.

seccions.titol: What can each option honestly show?
seccions.text: The three techniques start from different material. The project plans, a real photo of the room, or a description the model interprets on its own. The table sums up what you can honestly show with each one, what you need to commission it and which disclosure it needs, on portals, on your website or on the hoarding at the site.

seccions.titol: When is a 3D render the right choice?
seccions.text:
A 3D render makes sense when what you are selling cannot be photographed yet. That is the case for an off-plan development in Girona or a flat you want to show renovated. It is built from dimensioned plans, elevations, the specification and the real orientation, which is why you can stand behind it.
Before you commission it, settle what will be seen. Flooring, joinery, kitchen and the view from each window need to be decided, because in Catalonia what appears in advertising can be claimed by the buyer (Llei 18/2007, Article 58.4). At crida studio we start from the plans and the specification, and we put in writing what is final and what is indicative.

seccions.titol: When is virtual staging the right choice?
seccions.text:
Virtual staging makes sense when the flat already exists and is empty or furnished in a way that does not help. It is common with second homes on the Costa Brava that are sold or let empty. It starts from a real photo and adds furniture, curtains and light so that buyers understand the size of each room.
To commission it you need sharp, straight photos of each room, the real measurements and a list of what stays and what goes. The honest limit is furnishing. Hiding damp, changing windows or removing a column means showing a flat that does not exist. Publish the original photo next to the staged one.

seccions.titol: What does AI do well, and where does it still fail?
seccions.text:
AI is good for testing ideas in minutes. You can see three decoration styles for the same living room, change the time of day or prepare a mood image for social media. For internal use it is fast and good enough.
Where it fails is in what a buyer will later measure. It invents windows, moves doors, changes proportions and picks materials nobody chose. Many tools mix a 3D model with AI retouching, and the result can look like a reliable render without being one. Check every image against the plans before you publish it.

seccions.titol: What are the risks of showing something that does not exist?
seccions.text:
The first risk is legal. Catalonia’s Housing Act (Llei 18/2007) says that offers, promotion and advertising of homes must follow the principle of truthfulness and must not mislead buyers in a way that has economic consequences (Article 58.3). It also says that the data and features included in advertising can be claimed by the buyer later, even if they are not in the contract (Article 58.4).
The second risk is commercial. If the image promises light, a view or a kitchen that is not there, the viewing ends in disappointment. For new builds, the same act requires every advert to state whether the home is finished, under construction or only planned, and to give the usable and built floor areas (Article 59).

seccions.titol: What do you have to disclose in the listing and on your website?
seccions.text:
The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) applies from 2 August 2026 (Article 113). Article 50(4) says that deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake shall disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. A deployer is anyone using an AI system under their authority, except in a personal, non-professional activity (Article 3(4)).
The regulation defines a deep fake as AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful (Article 3(60)). If your image fits that definition, you have to disclose it. If you are not sure, disclose anyway. Put the notice on the image and in the listing text, even when the only change is virtual furniture.
Article 50(2) asks the providers of the tools to mark their outputs in a machine-readable format. If the tool was already on the market before 2 August 2026, its provider has until 2 December 2026 to comply (Article 111(4), added by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744). The European Commission has published a voluntary code of practice, guidelines on Article 50 and a set of icons for labelling such content.

seccions.titol: How to choose depending on the stage of the sale
seccions.text: Start with what exists today and who will see the image. These situations come up again and again in Girona and on the Costa Brava. If yours is a mix, combine techniques and disclose in every image what is not real.

faqs.q: I added virtual furniture to a real photo. Do I have to say so?
faqs.a: Always say so. If an AI tool placed it and the image could pass for real, Article 50(4) of the AI Act requires you to disclose that it was artificially manipulated. Article 50 only covers AI systems. If a person placed it with editing software and no AI, the Catalan Housing Act (Article 58.3) still requires you not to mislead buyers. Either way, say the furniture is virtual.

faqs.q: Does a 3D render made from the plans need an AI label too?
faqs.a: Article 50 covers content generated or manipulated by an AI system. A render calculated with 3D software from the plans is not, in principle, AI-generated content. If you then run it through an AI tool to change materials or add people and the result looks real, disclose it. For new builds, the Catalan Housing Act (Article 59) requires you to say whether the home is finished, under construction or planned.

faqs.q: How should the notice be shown so that it counts?
faqs.a: Article 50(5) of the regulation says the information must be provided in a clear and distinguishable manner, at the latest at the time of the first exposure. In practice, that means a short text on the image and a sentence in the listing description. The European Commission has published icons you can use. Keep the original photo in case someone asks for it.

whatsapp-business-app-api.intro: If you answer from your phone and get a handful of messages a day, the free WhatsApp Business app is enough. If several people need to reply, you want WhatsApp linked to your bookings or CRM, or you need answers out of hours, you need the WhatsApp Business Platform, which works through an API and is billed per message. Meta changed how it charges and its rules for automated assistants in 2026, so check them before you decide.

seccions.titol: What is the difference between the WhatsApp Business app and the API?
seccions.text:
The WhatsApp Business app is free and built for small businesses. You get a business profile, a catalogue, a greeting message and an away message, and you answer every conversation yourself from the phone. You set it up yourself in an afternoon.
The WhatsApp Business Platform is the same channel opened up through an API so other software can connect to it. You get in through a solution provider or a developer, several people can reply, and automated answers are possible. In return, Meta charges for every delivered message and asks you to follow its messaging policy.

seccions.titol: When is the WhatsApp Business app enough?
seccions.text:
It is enough when one person can answer everything that comes in within a reasonable time. Think of a hair salon in Salt or a restaurant in Palamós that writes bookings down by hand. If most messages are «do you have a table?» or «what time do you close?», the app covers it.
The limit comes when the phone becomes a bottleneck. If nobody knows who answered whom or summer multiplies the messages on the Costa Brava, the app no longer keeps the work in order and bookings start to slip through.

seccions.titol: When do you need the WhatsApp Business Platform or API?
seccions.text:
You need it when WhatsApp has to talk to other software or to more than one person at once. A clinic with three receptionists or a hotel confirming bookings from its property system cannot do that with a shared phone.
A hypothetical example, not a crida studio project. A small hotel in Begur gets availability questions at all hours. A system checks the bookings, replies with the free dates and, if the guest wants to book, alerts reception.

seccions.titol: How is the WhatsApp API billed?
seccions.text:
Meta has charged per delivered message since 1 July 2025, by message category and the customer’s country, and Spain has its own rate. Templates are marketing, utility or authentication. Free-form replies are service messages and can only be sent inside the 24-hour window that each customer message opens.
Since 1 October 2026, service messages are also charged once a number goes past a monthly free allowance, and utility messages sent as replies are no longer free. Meta says it only changes prices on the first day of a quarter. You will find no figures here. Check the official rate card and add the provider and the upkeep.

seccions.titol: Which rules does Meta set for automated assistants?
seccions.text:
You may automate replies inside the 24-hour window, but you must offer clear ways to reach a person. The WhatsApp Business Messaging Policy, updated on 23 September 2026, lists an in-chat transfer to a human agent, a phone number, an email, web support, an in-store visit or a support form.
Since 15 January 2026, Meta’s terms treat «AI Providers» separately, such as general-purpose AI assistants. They may only offer those where the law requires Meta to allow it, and Spain has been on that list since 11 March 2026. Meta says this does not change what it charges other businesses. If your assistant only serves your own customers, the messaging policy is what applies to you.

seccions.titol: What should you prepare before automating WhatsApp?
seccions.text:
Before connecting anything, sort out what you answer by hand today. Note the questions that repeat, the ones that need a person and the hours they arrive. Decide what the system may answer on its own, what it should prepare for someone to review and when it must raise a flag.
Conversations contain personal data. In its guidance on agentic AI from February 2026, the Spanish data protection authority (AEPD) recommends assessing the compliance of the service you contract, including article 28 of the GDPR, and effective human supervision, with people able to validate or overrule what the agent decides.

seccions.titol: Which mistakes should you avoid when moving to the API?
seccions.text:
The most expensive one is losing your conversations. To use a number from the app with the API, Meta explains you must either delete the account or onboard through a provider that supports app numbers. Delete it and the history is gone. With a provider that supports it, you can use the app and the provider’s tool at the same time and keep the history. Back up first.
Also avoid an assistant with no way out to a person, messages sent without opt-in and an account without a payment method, because Meta stops delivering the service messages it charges for. And do not copy prices from providers’ blogs.

faqs.q: Can I run a bot on the WhatsApp Business app without the API?
faqs.a: The app’s automated replies are fixed texts, such as the greeting and away messages. To answer based on what the customer asks or to check bookings you need the platform. Meta also offers its own AI agent, Meta Business Agent, with a category of its own on Meta’s rate card. If you try it, check how it hands the chat to a person and what it charges.

faqs.q: How much does a WhatsApp API message cost in Spain?
faqs.a: It depends on the category and the customer’s country, and Meta publishes the rate for Spain in its rate card. Since 1 July 2025 Meta charges per delivered message, and since 1 October 2026 service messages are also charged beyond a monthly allowance. This guide quotes no figures because Meta can change them every quarter. Check the official rate card.

faqs.q: Is it true that Meta has banned AI chatbots on WhatsApp since 2026?
faqs.a: Not for a business serving its own customers. Since 15 January 2026 Meta regulates general-purpose AI providers separately, and in Spain it allows them because the law requires it. What you must follow is the messaging policy, with automation inside the 24-hour window and clear ways to talk to a person.

estudi-webs-ajuntaments-girona.intro: Nearly every town council website in the province of Girona redirects to HTTPS and adapts to mobile, but 141 of 208 (67.8%) are missing a meta description, the text Google can show under the title. We analysed the home page of 208 of the 221 municipal websites on 30 and 31 October 2026. Only 30 of 208 (14.4%) pass all six basics at once.

seccions.titol: Only 30 of 208 town council websites pass all six basics at once
seccions.text:
The technical groundwork is done and what shows up in Google results is missing. Forced HTTPS, 200 of 207 sites (96.6%). Mobile viewport, 206 of 208 (99.0%). On the other hand, only 67 of 208 (32.2%) have a meta description, and 47 of 208 (22.6%) do not link to the accessibility statement from the home page.
141 of the 208 sites (67.8%) use the same WordPress theme, the one from the municipal websites platform of the Diputació de Girona, the provincial council. All 141 have a single H1 and structured data, 139 of 141 (98.6%) have an accessibility link and only 20 of 141 (14.2%) have a meta description.

seccions.titol: How we measured and what we could not measure
seccions.text:
A program of ours downloaded the home page of each official website on 30 and 31 October 2026 and read its HTML, without running JavaScript. The list of the 221 municipalities, with county, population on 1 January 2025 and official website, comes from the Generalitat’s open data (Municat), checked against Wikidata. It identifies itself as crida studio, respects robots.txt and makes at most one request per second to each server.
13 sites were left out, 4 with a domain that does not resolve, 3 with a 403 error, 3 with a 404 error, 2 that disallow robots in robots.txt and 1 that leads to a generic listing. None were forced. On 30 October the provincial council’s shared server, home to 143 of the 221 sites, stopped answering us after a burst of about three requests per second. The next day, at two seconds between requests, nothing was rejected.
This is not an audit. We only look at the home page HTML, so anything a site adds with JavaScript is invisible to us. We did not open any accessibility statement and we did not measure whether robots.txt blocks AI crawlers. The six-basics index is for comparing groups and is not a quality score. Groups with fewer than 8 sites are not compared.

seccions.titol: What happens in each county
seccions.text:
On the basics index the counties look alike. Among those that can be compared, with 8 or more sites analysed, the average runs from 5.2 in the Garrotxa to 4.7 in the Baix Empordà. Indicator by indicator there is more difference, and it depends mostly on how many sites in each county use the provincial council theme.
The Selva is the county where the fewest sites use that theme, 8 of 23 (34.8%), and the one with the most meta descriptions, 17 of 23 (73.9%). The Garrotxa, with 20 of 21 sites on the theme, is the only county where every site analysed links to accessibility from the home page.

seccions.titol: Small villages have more accessibility links and fewer meta descriptions
seccions.text:
In small villages almost every site is on the provincial council platform. Up to 500 residents, 75 of 79 sites (94.9%) use that theme, 75 of 79 (94.9%) have the accessibility link and only 9 of 79 (11.4%) have a meta description. Between 5,001 and 20,000 residents, where only 2 of 23 sites (8.7%) use the theme, it flips, a meta description in 16 of 23 (69.6%) and an accessibility link in 9 of 23 (39.1%).
In towns with over 20,000 residents none of the 10 sites uses the provincial council theme and only 1 of 10 is WordPress. They are the most likely to have a meta description, 8 of 10 (80.0%), but only 5 of 10 (50.0%) have a single H1.

seccions.titol: 47 sites do not link to the accessibility statement from the home page
seccions.text:
161 of the 208 sites analysed (77.4%) have a link on the home page with the word accessibility. The other 47 of 208 (22.6%) do not. Spain’s Royal Decree 1112/2018, in article 15.1, says the statement must be reachable from every page through a link labelled “Accessibility” and must be updated at least once a year.
If the link is not on the home page, it is not on every page. Among the 141 sites on the provincial council theme, 139 (98.6%) have the link. Among the other 67 sites, only 22 (32.8%) do. We did not open any statement, so we do not know whether it exists, whether it is up to date or whether the site is actually accessible.

seccions.titol: What a town council can do with this data
seccions.text:
Many of the missing items can be fixed from the content management system, without changing the website. The list lets you review your council’s home page with the same criteria as the study. If the site is on the provincial council platform, first check what the editor lets you change.
The aggregates by county and by population band can be downloaded as CSV from the links below, with no data on individual councils. If you work for the council and want to know how your site did, ask us through the contact form.

faqs.q: Can I find out how my council’s website did?
faqs.a: Yes, if you work for the council. The page and the CSV files only contain aggregates by county and by population band, because the study is not meant to single out any council. Ask us through the contact form and we will explain what we saw on your home page, without publishing it anywhere.

faqs.q: How often will the study be repeated?
faqs.a: There is no date yet. When we repeat it we want to add what this one could not see, how many sites block AI crawlers in robots.txt, the date of each accessibility statement and an inner page. We will keep the same slow pace and publish the new figures with the same base, compared with October 2026.

faqs.q: How was each website measured?
faqs.a: With a program that downloads the home page of each municipality’s official website, reads its HTML and looks for a fixed set of indicators, such as the meta description, the number of H1 tags or the accessibility link. It does not run JavaScript, identifies itself as crida studio and respects robots.txt.

xatbot-ia-avisar-llei.intro: Yes. Since 2 August 2026, Article 50 of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act applies. It says AI systems built to interact directly with people must be designed so the person knows they are dealing with AI, unless that is obvious. If you run a chatbot on your website, a WhatsApp bot or a voice assistant on the phone, it is time to check what your customer sees in the very first message.

seccions.titol: What the law says and since when
seccions.text:
Article 50(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 requires providers to make sure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed so those people are informed they are interacting with an AI system. The only general exception is when this is obvious to a reasonably well-informed and observant person, given the context.
Article 113 sets the general date of application at 2 August 2026. The European Commission confirms this in its FAQ on Article 50 and published guidelines on 20 July 2026 to help apply it. The current wording of the article is available on the Commission's AI Act Service Desk.
The Commission published the final version of the guidelines, dated 5 November 2026, reference C(2026) 7702. It makes clear that chatbots already running before 2 August 2026 must also disclose from that day. The 2 December 2026 deadline only applies to marking generated content.
On 12 November 2026 the Official Journal of the European Union published the same guidelines as Communication C/2026/6005. It is the same document, with the same title and the same 155 paragraphs, so paragraph 153 cited in this guide is the same in both versions.

seccions.titol: What changes for chatbots on 2 December 2026
seccions.text:
For the disclosure, nothing changes. Telling customers they are talking to an AI has been mandatory since 2 August 2026, including for chatbots that were already running before then. The Commission guidelines say so in point 153. Systems that both chat and generate content only get extra time for a different obligation, marking.
2 December 2026 is the deadline for marking. Article 111(4), added by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, gives providers of systems that generate audio, images, video or text and were placed on the market before 2 August 2026 until that day to comply with Article 50(2). It means their output has to be marked in a machine-readable format.
If your chatbot also generates content, such as text or images, marking is the provider's job. Ask them in writing whether they already do it and since when, and keep the reply. If you built the chatbot yourself and run it under your own name, the obligation is yours. For images and text you publish, see how to label AI-generated content.

seccions.titol: Which businesses this really affects
seccions.text:
Anyone with an AI system talking to customers. The Commission's examples are chatbots, AI agents and avatars. Think of a clinic in Girona answering on WhatsApp through a bot, or a restaurant on the Costa Brava handling bookings with an assistant.
The Regulation separates two roles. The provider is whoever develops the system and places it on the market under its own name (Article 3(3)). The deployer is whoever uses it under its own authority (Article 3(4)). The duty in Article 50(1) sits with the provider, but the notice is what your customer sees on your website, so it is worth checking it yourself.
The "obvious" exception exists, but the Commission says in its FAQ that it should be interpreted restrictively. If your chatbot has a person's name and writes like a person, the safe choice is to show the notice.

seccions.titol: What the notice has to look like
seccions.text:
Article 50(5) requires the information to be clear and distinguishable, at the latest at the first interaction, and to meet the applicable accessibility requirements. It does not prescribe wording or design. That is up to you, as long as it arrives at that first interaction. In practice, three things together work well.
Do not bury it in the privacy policy alone. The rule talks about the first interaction, and nobody reads a privacy policy before asking for opening hours or whether there is a table free for dinner.

seccions.titol: What if you use AI to write copy or make images
seccions.text:
Article 50 also covers generated content. Paragraph 2 requires providers of tools that generate text, images, audio or video to mark their output in a machine-readable format. The Commission explains that tools already on the market before 2 August 2026 have until 2 December 2026 to comply.
Paragraph 4 does concern you if you publish. Anyone using AI to generate or manipulate images, audio or video that amount to a deepfake must disclose that the content is artificial. And anyone publishing AI-generated text to inform the public on matters of public interest must say so, unless a person has reviewed it and someone holds editorial responsibility.
Article 50(4) only covers deepfakes and text on matters of public interest. A product sheet or a sales email is not mentioned there. A town council publishing news items would do well to record in writing who reviews the text and who is responsible for it.

seccions.titol: What happens if you do not comply
seccions.text:
Article 99(4)(g) lists the transparency obligations of Article 50 among those that can be fined with up to 15 million euros or, for a company, up to 3 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the previous financial year, whichever is higher. Article 99(6) says that for SMEs, including start-ups, the lower of the two figures applies.
Article 99(7) lists what is weighed when setting a fine, such as the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement and its consequences, the size and annual turnover of the company and whether it was intentional or negligent.

seccions.titol: What to check this week
seccions.text: If you have AI talking to customers, this list takes an afternoon. Just open the chatbot the way a new customer would, write down what they see and ask your provider about anything you cannot check yourself.

seccions.titol: EU AI Act chatbot disclosure at a glance
seccions.text:
If you only have a minute, this table sums up what Article 50 says about chatbots and what the Commission's final guidelines add. Where it says point, it means the paragraph number in the guidelines document C(2026) 7702.
If you bought the chatbot from a company that sells it under its own name, that company is the provider. If you built it yourself, or took someone else's system and modified it, for example with new training data, and you run it under your own name, the guidelines say you become the provider. The duty to design the notice is then yours.

seccions.titol: Example disclosure texts you can copy
seccions.text:
The guidelines give examples such as a label saying «You are interacting with an AI system», a greeting in the chatbot's first message and, on the phone, an opening line like «This is an AI-powered assistant». They also expect the system to say it is AI whenever someone asks. Adapt these texts to the tone of your business.
Avoid vague signals. According to the guidelines, a bare «assistant» label is not enough, and neither are technical lines such as «this system uses LLMs». With older people, children or sensitive topics such as health, insurance or complaints, they recommend reminding people now and then during the conversation.

faqs.q: My chatbot only has scripted answers, no AI. Does this apply to me?
faqs.a: The Regulation talks about AI systems as defined in Article 3(1). A fixed question tree that neither learns nor generates text may not fit that definition, but your tool provider has to confirm that. If in doubt, show the notice anyway. It costs one sentence.

faqs.q: I bought the chatbot from an outside company. Who is responsible?
faqs.a: Article 50(1) puts the duty to design the notice on the system's provider, and you are the deployer under Article 3(4). But the notice appears on your website and talks to your customers. Ask the provider how they comply, check it yourself and keep their answer in writing.

faqs.q: Is it enough to explain it in the privacy policy?
faqs.a: Article 50(5) says the information must be clear and distinguishable and reach the person at the latest at the first interaction. A sentence inside a legal page is not what the customer sees when they open the chat. Put it in the first message and in the chat window.

faqs.q: Does a voice assistant on the phone have to say it too?
faqs.a: Article 50(1) does not mention specific channels. It speaks of AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons, wherever that happens. If an AI-generated voice answers your phone, the simplest route is for the first sentence to say so and offer to pass the call to a person.

faqs.q: Can a chatbot be the only customer service channel?
faqs.a: In Spain, Law 10/2025 on customer service says no, but only for the companies covered by its Article 2. These are providers of basic services (water, gas, electricity, passenger transport, postal services, telecommunications and financial services) and companies that sell mainly to consumers and, in the previous financial year, alone or within their group, had at least 250 employees, turnover above €50 million or a balance sheet above €43 million. For them, Article 8.1 bans automated answering systems or similar tools as the only channel, Article 3.11 requires service by a person, not an automatic one, when the customer asks, and Article 8.2 requires the chatbot to offer a person at any point in the conversation. They have until 28 December 2026 to adapt.

verifactu-programa-facturacio.intro: Under the BOE text in force on 11 November 2026, invoicing software in Spain must be Verifactu-ready before 1 January 2027 for companies paying corporate tax and before 1 July 2027 for the self-employed and everyone else. Verifactu is the everyday name for Royal Decree 1007/2023. On 5 October 2026 the Treasury announced it plans to move the deadline to October 2028, but that is not yet in the BOE.

seccions.titol: What Verifactu is and what it asks of your invoicing software
seccions.text:
Verifactu is shorthand for the regulation approved by Royal Decree 1007/2023, as the Spanish tax agency (AEAT) explains in its own FAQ. The regulation does not change what an invoice looks like. It sets requirements for the software that produces it, which the rule calls an invoicing computer system.
Article 8 requires the software to guarantee the integrity, preservation, accessibility, legibility, traceability and unalterability of invoicing records. Every invoice produces a record with a hash, chained to the previous one, that cannot be deleted or edited without the software detecting it. The software must be able to send those records to the tax agency (article 8.1). Each invoice carries a QR code, under the first final provision of the decree, which adds it to the invoicing regulation.

seccions.titol: Who it applies to and who is left out
seccions.text:
Article 3.1 covers companies paying Spanish corporate tax and self-employed people with a business activity, among others, as long as they use software to invoice, even for only part of their activity. A restaurant in Girona with a POS, a clinic with practice software or a property developer invoicing from an ERP all fall inside.
Article 3.3 leaves out taxpayers who keep their VAT ledgers through the AEAT online office, the system known as SII. The AEAT sums it up as the rule of four noes. It does not apply to anyone who invoices entirely by hand, anyone on the SII, anyone whose tax domicile is in the Basque Country or Navarre, or anyone with a non-application ruling.

seccions.titol: When it becomes mandatory. What the law says and what the Treasury has announced
seccions.text:
The fourth final provision of Royal Decree 1007/2023, as worded by Royal Decree-Law 15/2025, says corporate taxpayers must have their software adapted before 1 January 2027 and all other obliged taxpayers before 1 July 2027. As of 11 November 2026, that is the text published in the Spanish official gazette, the BOE.
On 5 October 2026 the Ministry of Finance published a note saying it plans to postpone the pending obligations of the regulation to October 2028, so they coincide with mandatory electronic invoicing for anyone invoicing up to 8 million euros a year. The note says the technical requirements will remain substantially equivalent.
Until that postponement appears in the BOE, the 2027 dates are the ones that count. The AEAT describes the period before them as a testing period. You can send test records with Verifactu software and keep invoicing with another program until the deadline.

seccions.titol: Two ways to comply. Send records to the AEAT or keep them signed
seccions.text:
The regulation allows two kinds of software. The first sends every invoicing record to the tax agency continuously and automatically. Article 16 calls it a verifiable invoice issuing system, or Verifactu system. It is presumed to meet article 8 and does not need to sign each record electronically. Calculating the hash is enough.
The second kind sends nothing to the AEAT. In that case the software must electronically sign every creation and cancellation record (article 12). Both kinds must have a secure download and archiving procedure for the records (article 8.2.c). Invoices issued with a Verifactu system carry the phrase «Factura verificable en la sede electrónica de la AEAT» or «VERI*FACTU». If you start sending records systematically, you are deemed to have chosen Verifactu (article 16.5).

seccions.titol: What to ask your software vendor this quarter
seccions.text:
The software producer must certify with a responsible declaration that the product meets the regulation (article 13). It has to appear in writing and visibly inside the software, in every version, and you are entitled to ask for it. If your vendor cannot show it to you, you have a problem. These are the questions to ask now.
The AEAT recommends asking the vendor first whether an adapted version exists, and otherwise considering another program, its own free invoicing application or an in-house development. The AEAT application is option b of article 7 and counts as a Verifactu system (article 16.4).

seccions.titol: What happens to the old software and what the penalty is
seccions.text:
Article 201 bis.2 of the Spanish General Tax Law, quoted in the AEAT FAQ, penalises holding invoicing software that is not certified when it should be, with a fixed fine of 50,000 euros per financial year. The same answer lets you keep the old program to look up past invoices if you can show it can no longer issue them. If after the deadline it can still invoice, the AEAT says merely holding it would be an infringement.
For a small business this is a good moment to tidy up the whole process. If quotes come out of one tool, invoices out of another and payments out of a third, adapting to Verifactu is the excuse to connect them. That is how we approach it when we automate processes.

faqs.q: I make my invoices in Excel or Word. Does Verifactu apply to me?
faqs.a: It depends on what you do with them. According to the AEAT FAQ, if Excel or Word are used only to enter the data, issue and print the invoices and keep them, the regulation does not apply. If you also use them to generate your VAT ledgers or your accounts, for example with a macro, they count as an invoicing computer system. Check with your accountant.

faqs.q: If the Treasury postpones it to 2028, can I wait?
faqs.a: The Treasury note of 5 October 2026 is a forecast and has not yet changed the BOE. Until it is published, the legal date is 2027. The same note says the technical requirements will remain. Whatever you do now to adapt your software is useful whether or not the postponement goes ahead.

faqs.q: I am on the SII or my tax domicile is in the Basque Country or Navarre. Does it apply?
faqs.a: No. Article 3.3 of the regulation excludes taxpayers who keep their VAT ledgers through the AEAT online office, which is the SII. And the AEAT rule of four noes includes having your tax domicile in the Basque Country or Navarre, which run their own systems. If you are not sure whether you are on the SII, your accountant will know.

faqs.q: Do I need to change software or is an update enough?
faqs.a: It depends on the vendor. The AEAT recommends asking them first whether an adapted version exists, as that is the most common case. If there is none, the options it lists are another adapted program, its own free application or an in-house development. In every case, ask for the article 13 responsible declaration before paying.

estudi-webs-allotjaments-girona.intro: Most accommodation websites in the province of Girona invite visitors to book directly and offer two or more languages, while a minority tell Google what kind of lodging they are. We analysed the home page of 675 websites of hotels, campsites, rural houses, guesthouses and tourist apartments on 31 October and 1 November 2026. 487 (72.1%) have a booking engine or button, 515 (76.3%) two or more languages and 103 (15.3%) lodging structured data.

seccions.titol: What the figures from 675 Girona accommodation websites say
seccions.text:
Most sites analysed invite visitors to book without going through a portal. 487 of 675 (72.1%) have a booking engine or a booking button on the home page, and 73 (10.8%) link to a booking portal such as Booking or Tripadvisor. 515 (76.3%) offer two or more languages. Meanwhile, 103 (15.3%) tell Google through structured data that they are a hotel, a campsite or a rural house.
The basics do not go together. 584 of 675 (86.5%) redirect on their own to HTTPS and 617 (91.4%) adapt to mobile, but 364 (53.9%) have exactly one H1 and 33 (4.9%) pass all six basics at once. The six-basics index, the same one used in the town council website study, averages 4.01.

seccions.titol: How we measured and what we could not measure
seccions.text:
We start from two official sources. The Catalonia Tourism Register, open data from the Generalitat, lists 2,160 accommodation establishments in the province of Girona, not counting tourist-use homes, but has no website field. We took each website from the establishment’s listing on catalunya.com, the Catalan Tourist Board’s website, which covers 1,943 of them (90.0%). 1,301 listings carry their own website, adding up to 1,037 distinct sites because 147 are shared.
A program of ours downloaded the home page of each site on 31 October and 1 November 2026 and read its HTML without running JavaScript, with the same method as the town council study. It analysed 675 of 1,037 (65.1%). Of the other 362, 194 have a domain that does not resolve, 46 answer 403, 39 disallow robots and the other 83 are empty or parked, lead to another platform, do not respond or return an error.
This is neither a census nor an audit. A property may have a website even if its catalunya.com listing shows none, and domains that do not resolve reflect the listing, not the establishment. Whatever a site adds with JavaScript, such as many booking engines and language switchers, is invisible to us, so these figures are minimums. The two indexes are our own criteria for comparing groups, not quality scores. Groups with fewer than 8 sites are not compared.

seccions.titol: How bookings work on Girona accommodation websites
seccions.text:
487 of 675 sites (72.1%) have a booking engine or a direct booking button on the home page. On 196 (29.0%) we identified the engine by name, such as Mirai, Avirato, SiteMinder, Thelis or WitBooking, and on 291 (43.1%) there is an identified engine or a booking subdomain. The other 196 (29.0%) only have a booking button or link, which may lead to an engine loaded with JavaScript or to a contact form.
Booking portals rarely appear on home pages. 73 of 675 (10.8%) link to an OTA, 62 (9.2%) to Tripadvisor and 16 (2.4%) to Booking.com. 13 sites (1.9%) link to a portal and have no engine or button of their own. 379 (56.1%) have WhatsApp or a clickable phone number, and 210 (31.1%) show prices or a date search.
The direct sales index, our own criterion from 0 to 4, gives one point each for a booking engine or button, two or more languages, WhatsApp or a clickable phone number, and prices or a date search. The average is 2.36 and 123 of 675 sites (18.2%) score all four points. By type, over the sites analysed in each, a booking engine or button ranges from 83.2% of campsites to 54.8% of guesthouses.

seccions.titol: Which languages the sites offer and which they are written in
seccions.text:
515 of 675 sites (76.3%) offer two or more languages, counting the language switcher and hreflang tags. Spanish is on 501 (74.2%), English on 479 (71.0%), Catalan on 459 (68.0%), French on 418 (61.9%), German on 161 (23.9%) and Dutch on 90 (13.3%). 415 (61.5%) have hreflang, the tag that tells Google the version for each language.
The home page is declared in Catalan on 315 of 675 sites (46.7%) and in Spanish on 220 (32.6%), and 73 (10.8%) declare no language. On the Costa Brava, 402 of 503 sites (79.9%) offer two or more languages, and in the Pyrenees brand (Pirineus) 110 of 164 (67.1%). By county, that figure runs from 83.2% in the Selva to 63.8% in the Garrotxa, leaving aside Osona, which has only 8 sites.

seccions.titol: The technical basics and what Google can read
seccions.text:
33 of 675 sites (4.9%) pass all six basics at once, forced HTTPS, viewport, meta description, a single H1, declared language and accessibility link, and 272 (40.3%) pass five or six. The least common indicator is the accessibility link, 42 of 675 (6.2%), followed by the single H1, 192 sites (28.4%) have none and 119 (17.6%) have more than one.
386 of 675 (57.2%) carry structured data (JSON-LD). 103 (15.3% of the 675) use it to say they are a lodging, with a type such as Hotel (63 sites), LodgingBusiness (24) or Campground (21). The most common types are Organization (248), WebSite (243) and BreadcrumbList (196), which describe the website rather than the kind of business.
Compared with the 208 Girona town council websites we analysed in October 2026 with the same method, accommodation sites have more meta descriptions (73.6% against 32.2%) and far more hreflang (61.5% against 3.4%), and fewer accessibility links (6.2% against 77.4%) and fewer six-basics passes (4.9% against 14.4%). The accessibility obligations of a town council and a private company are not the same, and the link is counted only for comparison.

seccions.titol: What an accommodation business can do with this data
seccions.text:
The list lets you review your property’s home page with the study’s criteria. Almost everything can be checked by opening the site on a phone and, if needed, the page source, and many items can be fixed from the content management system or from the booking engine. Our guide on rural tourism websites explains how to make direct booking easier.
The aggregates by county, type of accommodation, category, population band (on 1 January 2025, from Municat) and tourist brand can be downloaded as CSV from the links below, with no data on individual establishments, in case you want to compare your group or redo the sums.

seccions.titol: A direct booking example
seccions.text: Can Junqué, a rural holiday home in Ullà, sells its stays on its own website. Visitors pick their dates, see which units are free and book and pay without leaving the site, and the calendar is synced with Airbnb and Booking so no night is sold twice.

faqs.q: Can I find out how my property’s website did?
faqs.a: Yes, if you run the establishment. The page and the CSV files only contain aggregates by county, type, category, population band and tourist brand, because the study is not meant to single out any property. Ask us through the contact form and we will explain what we saw on your home page, without publishing it anywhere.

faqs.q: Why is my website not in the study?
faqs.a: Because it only covers the websites shown in the catalunya.com listings of establishments registered in the Tourism Register, excluding tourist-use homes. If the listing has no website, shows an old one or the site keeps robots out, it was not analysed. Hostels and mountain refuges are not included either.

faqs.q: What does the direct sales index mean?
faqs.a: It is our criterion, from 0 to 4. It gives one point for each thing that helps guests book without a portal, a booking engine or button, two or more languages, WhatsApp or a clickable phone number, and prices or a date search. It does not say whether a site sells well or badly, only how many of these tools are visible.

faqs.q: How was each website measured?
faqs.a: With a program that downloads the home page of each site, reads its HTML and looks for a fixed set of indicators, such as the booking engine, the languages, the meta description or the structured data. It does not run JavaScript, identifies itself as crida studio, respects robots.txt and makes at most one request per second to each server.

ressenyes-google.intro: Ask every customer for a review right after the service, using the link or QR code from your Business Profile. Google allows this as long as you offer nothing in return and don't try to steer the rating or the wording. If you pay or give discounts for reviews, Google removes them and can stop your profile from getting new ones for a while.

seccions.titol: Why reviews help you show up on Google Maps
seccions.text:
Reviews count towards local search. Google says local results are mainly based on relevance, distance and prominence. Prominence means how well known a business is. To judge it, Google looks at, among other things, how many reviews you have. It also says that more reviews and positive ratings can help your local ranking.
Google also says there is no way to pay for a better local ranking. For a shop in Lloret de Mar or a clinic in Girona, that means earning reviews one customer at a time. A complete, up-to-date profile matters too. With your address, opening hours and category filled in, Google has a clearer idea of what you do and which searches to show you in.

seccions.titol: How to ask customers for reviews
seccions.text:
From your Business Profile you can create a link and a QR code to ask for reviews. Google recommends using them to remind customers they can leave a review. Ask everyone with the same short, neutral message, such as “It would really help us if you told Google how it went”. Don't mention the rating you hope for or what you want them to say.
The best moment is right after the service, while the experience is still fresh. That way you don't have to chase people weeks later. Put the link wherever customers already hear from you, for example in these places.

seccions.titol: What Google bans when you ask for reviews
seccions.text:
The basic rule is that every review must come from a genuine experience. That is why Google bans offering payments, discounts or free products and services in exchange for a review. You also can't offer anything to get a customer to change or remove a negative one. If you have front-of-house staff, explain these rules to them.
Google Maps rules also limit how you ask for reviews, even when no gift is involved. For example, you can't ask your staff to bring in a set number of reviews. You also can't do any of the following.

seccions.titol: What happens if Google finds fake or paid reviews
seccions.text:
Google removes reviews that break its rules, such as those written by an employee or a relative. If it finds that a business has bought reviews, made them up or got them by offering something in return, it can also restrict the profile. For example, for a set period it can stop the profile from receiving new reviews or hide the ones it already has. It can also show a warning that fake reviews were removed.
Google emails the owner if it plans to apply a restriction, and the business can appeal if it thinks Google got it wrong. For a restaurant or hotel on the Costa Brava, losing visible reviews in the middle of the season is not a risk worth taking.
In Spain, article 27.8 of the Unfair Competition Act (Law 3/1991) also classes as misleading, and therefore unfair, any practice that adds fake consumer reviews or endorsements, or gets another natural or legal person to add them, or distorts consumer reviews or social endorsements in order to promote goods or services. This provision has been in force since 28 May 2022.

seccions.titol: How to reply to reviews, including the bad ones
seccions.text:
Replies are public, so keep them short, polite and written for each review. Google suggests not sending everyone the same thank you and not using replies to push deals, since the reviewer is already a customer. Reply promptly and sign off with your name or initials.
When a review is negative, never share the customer's personal details and don't attack them. Acknowledge what went wrong, explain what you can and can't do, and apologise where it makes sense. If the situation is complicated, invite them to sort it out by phone or email.

seccions.titol: What to do about a fake or unfair review
seccions.text:
If you think a review breaks Google's rules, you can flag it so Google can check it. That applies, for example, to reviews posted by a competitor to harm you or not based on a real experience. It also applies to offensive reviews and to ones that share someone's personal details without consent.
On the other hand, Google allows reviews that describe a bad experience respectfully. In that case, the right move is a good reply. Google itself notes that a mix of positive and negative feedback often feels more trustworthy.

faqs.q: Can I give a discount to customers who leave a Google review?
faqs.a: No. Google treats a discount in exchange for a review as fake engagement and bans it, just like payments or free products. If it finds out, Google removes those reviews and can restrict the profile. You can still ask for reviews, just without offering anything in return.

faqs.q: Do customers need a Google Account to leave a review?
faqs.a: Yes. People must be signed in to a Google Account to write a review. But Google explains that customers can create one with an email address that isn't Gmail. If many of your customers don't have an account, mention this in the message where you ask for the review.

faqs.q: Can my staff or family leave reviews for the business?
faqs.a: They shouldn't. Google Maps rules don't allow reviews based on a conflict of interest, such as current or former employment at the business or family relationships. Google removes them when it detects them. Your team can still remind customers that they are welcome to leave one.

faqs.q: Can I ask a customer to change a negative review?
faqs.a: The best approach is to reply well and try to fix the problem. Google says a helpful reply and follow-up may even encourage the customer to update their review. What you can't do is offer anything in exchange for changing or removing it, because Google Maps rules explicitly ban that.

fitxa-google-business-profile.intro: To show up on Google Maps, you need to create or claim your Google Business Profile and get it verified. Then pick the most specific category and say whether customers come to you or you go to them. Fill in services, hours and photos, using the same name, address and phone number as on your website. Google says you can't pay to rank higher in local results. In the Performance section you can measure searches, views, calls, directions and clicks.

seccions.titol: Before you create a profile, search for your business and pick a type
seccions.text:
Start by searching Google for your business name and town. If the profile exists and nobody has claimed it, claim it. If it isn't there, add it with a Google Account, which you can open with any email address, not just Gmail.
Next, decide how you serve customers. If you have premises with permanent signage, the profile shows your address. If you travel to customers, like a plumber, you hide the address and set a service area. Google says that area generally shouldn't stretch beyond about two hours' drive from your base. If you do both, like a restaurant that also delivers, you're a hybrid business.

seccions.titol: Which category to choose for your profile
seccions.text:
The category tells Google and customers what your business is. Choose the most specific one on the list and use as few as you need to describe your core business. Google suggests a simple test. The category should complete the sentence “this business is”, not “this business has”.
Say you run a hotel in Tossa de Mar with a pool. The category is Hotel, not Swimming pool. Don't use categories as keywords, and don't add the category of a business operating inside yours, like the hotel bar if another company runs it. If you can't find your category, pick a more general one.

seccions.titol: What to fill in so your profile is complete
seccions.text:
Google says businesses with complete and accurate information are more likely to show up in local results. If something is wrong, your profile may not appear for relevant searches in your area. Fill in these sections and check them again whenever something changes.
Some businesses, such as hotels, schools or cinemas, shouldn't list hours at all. Reviews also help you show up on Maps. To learn how to ask for them without breaking the rules, read the reviews guide linked below.

seccions.titol: How to verify your profile, including by video
seccions.text:
Until your profile is verified, you can't edit it or see how many people view it. Google decides which verification methods you get, and you can't change them. They may include a phone call or text, an email, a live video call, a postcard with a code or a video you record yourself. If video is offered, Google recommends using it.
Record the video live on your phone, from within the profile. It must be at least 30 seconds long and shot in one continuous take, with no cuts or pauses. Keep other people's faces and private details, such as ID or bank numbers, out of shot. Google can take up to five business days to review it. Before you hit record, plan how you'll show these three things.

seccions.titol: Your name, address and phone number should match your website
seccions.text:
The profile name must be your real business name, the one on your sign, website and stationery. The address must be exact. The phone number must be one you control that rings at that business. A local number is better than a call centre line, and premium-rate numbers are never allowed.
For the website, use your own site rather than a social media page. Put the same name, address and phone number on your contact page and footer as on the profile. Google says that when it ranks local results, it also looks at how many websites link to your business.

seccions.titol: What not to do with your Business Profile
seccions.text:
Google can suspend a profile that breaks its guidelines. For example, if a carpentry workshop's sign only shows its name, don't add “custom furniture Girona” to the name on its profile. These are the mistakes Google won't accept.
Watch out for duplicates too. Google says there should only be one profile per business. A doctor shouldn't have a separate profile for each specialty either. Duplicates can make your information show up wrong on Maps. If you find an old listing, claim it instead of creating a new one.

seccions.titol: What you can measure in Google Business Profile to see if it brings customers
seccions.text:
Once your profile is verified, the Performance section shows how people find you on Search and Maps and what they do next. You can pick the dates you want to look at. The figures cover both organic results and Google Ads.
Focus on calls, directions and clicks, because those are people who want to visit or get in touch. If your business is seasonal, like so many on the Costa Brava, compare each month with the same month last year.
You can download the data as a spreadsheet from Business Profile Manager, including several profiles at once to compare locations. Google notes that you will only see the metrics that apply to your business. Some profiles also have an Insights section with recommendations based on reviews, photos and local search trends.

faqs.q: Can I have a Business Profile if I work from home?
faqs.a: Yes, as a service-area business. Google says that if you don't serve customers at your address, you should hide it and list the areas you cover. To verify by video, you can film street signs and landmarks in your neighbourhood.

faqs.q: How long does Google take to verify a profile?
faqs.a: Google says it can take up to five business days to review your verification, and on rare occasions longer. If you get a postcard, most codes arrive within 14 days and expire after 30 days. While you wait, don't change your business name, address or category, or the code won't work.

faqs.q: Can I have a Business Profile if I only sell online?
faqs.a: No. Google says online-only businesses, such as e-commerce shops with no in-person service, aren't eligible for a Business Profile. If you also have premises where you serve customers, the profile is for that location, and your website handles the online sales.

faqs.q: What is my profile’s Place ID and what is it for?
faqs.a: It is the identifier Google uses for your business on Maps, a code that is unique to each place. You can find it with Google’s Place ID Finder. Some tools and developers ask for it to connect a website or an app to your profile. Google warns that it can change over time and recommends looking it up again if you saved it more than a year ago.

faqs.q: What can you measure in Google Business Profile?
faqs.a: The Performance section shows searches, with the terms people used, and views of your profile. It also shows calls, direction requests, website clicks, messages and bookings. You can pick the dates, and the figures combine organic results and Google Ads.

xatbot-en-catala.intro: Yes, you can run an AI chatbot that replies in Catalan on your website or WhatsApp, because today's large models understand and write it. Google and OpenAI both list Catalan, but neither gives a quality score, and OpenAI's voices are optimised for English. Before you go live, test it with real customer questions, decide how it switches language, check where the data goes and say clearly that it is AI.

seccions.titol: How well today's AI models handle Catalan
seccions.text:
The big models understand and write Catalan. Google lists it among the languages every Gemini model understands, according to documentation updated on 30 October 2026, and OpenAI includes it in the list for its speech models. Neither list gives a quality score for each language.
Anthropic publishes a table of Claude's results in fourteen languages, measured against English. Catalan is not in it. Anthropic says Claude works in many more languages than the ones in the table and recommends testing it in the ones you use.
For a shop, hotel or town council in Catalonia, Catalan is supported but the quality is yours to check. If you would rather use an open model built for Catalan, the Aina project, led by the Government of Catalonia with the Barcelona Supercomputing Center, publishes them.

seccions.titol: How the chatbot should switch language
seccions.text:
The simplest rule is to reply in the customer's language and switch when they do. Claude infers the language from the conversation, but Anthropic recommends stating it in the system prompt so the rule holds for the whole chat. If customers pick a language with a button, that choice goes into the prompt too.
Settle the grey areas in advance. One Spanish word in a Catalan message is not a change of language. A visitor on the Costa Brava writing in English is. And the opening message should match the language of the page the customer is on.
Article 128-1 of the Catalan Consumer Code says consumers are entitled to be served, orally and in writing, in whichever official language they choose. According to ruling 88/2017 of Spain's Constitutional Court, this paragraph does not create a true consumer right or a language availability duty for businesses, because it defers to language legislation. Even so, someone who writes to you in Catalan expects a reply in Catalan.

seccions.titol: Voice or text. What changes when the chatbot speaks
seccions.text:
Start with text, which is easier to test and correct. Voice adds two more pieces, one that turns what the customer says into text and one that reads the answer aloud. Either can stumble in Catalan even when the model writes it well.
OpenAI supports Catalan in its speech models but warns that its voices are optimised for English. A voice like that may sound foreign or mispronounce names such as Sant Feliu de Guíxols. The Aina project also produces resources so that voice assistants can work in Catalan.
If your customers send voice notes on WhatsApp, the system has to transcribe them. Test with older callers, background noise and regional accents, and always leave a way to carry on in writing. Ona, the assistant on the crida studio website, speaks the language of the page, switches if you talk to her in another one and, if the voice fails, lets you keep typing.

seccions.titol: How to test it before it goes live
seccions.text:
Make a list of the real questions from a normal month, from WhatsApp, email and the phone. Write them the way people do, with typos and mixed languages. Then read the answers aloud with a Catalan speaker on your team. If a customer from Girona would never put it that way, fix it.
Also test what the chatbot does not know, such as a bank holiday, a price that is not in the sources or a booking. Look out above all for made-up answers, confirmations of things it has not done and slips into Spanish. The table gives a few examples to start with. Adapt them to your business.

seccions.titol: What data the chatbot keeps and where it goes
seccions.text:
Every conversation can contain personal data. Customers may type their name, phone number or a health problem without anyone asking. Before you sign up for a tool, put the questions below to the provider and explain the answers in the privacy policy on your website.
Limit what the chatbot asks for, too. A clinic does not need the bot to collect symptoms to book an appointment, and a town council does not need an ID number to give the recycling centre's opening hours. If an outside company runs the tool, ask for a data processing agreement before launch.

seccions.titol: It must say it is AI, in Catalan too
seccions.text:
Our guide on AI chatbot disclosure explains when and how to tell people they are talking to an AI. Here we only add the language side. The notice should appear in the language of the conversation and is worth repeating if the customer switches language.
Voice works the same way. OpenAI's usage policies require a clear disclosure that the voice people hear is AI-generated. On the phone or in a voice note, the first sentence can say so in Catalan and offer to pass the customer to someone on the team.

faqs.q: Which AI model is best at Catalan?
faqs.a: The language pages from Google, OpenAI and Anthropic do not give a separate score for Catalan. The reliable way to choose is to run the same real questions through two or three models. Ask someone on your team who writes good Catalan to compare the answers and note the mistakes.

faqs.q: Can I make the chatbot answer only in Catalan?
faqs.a: Yes, one line in the instructions does it. But think about customers who do not understand it. Some will write to you in Spanish and, on the Costa Brava, in English too. If the bot only answers in Catalan, those customers get no answer. A good option is to open in Catalan and follow the customer's lead.

faqs.q: Do I need a model made in Catalonia, like the Aina ones?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, because commercial models already understand Catalan. Aina's open models make sense if you want to run the model on your own servers or need a specific Catalan component, such as voice. Either way, testing with real questions from your customers is what settles it.

faqs.q: What should I do if the chatbot gets something wrong after launch?
faqs.a: First check where the answer came from. If it made up opening hours, maybe they were missing from the sources or only there in Spanish. Fix the source, add the question to your test list and run it again. And agree with the provider how often you will review the conversations.

bio-analisi-mercat-equip-nou.intro: A market analysis for new equipment has to answer who will buy it, for which modality and scale, against which alternative, and how many units you can realistically sell. You build it by combining public data, such as the AseBio and Biocat reports, interviews with buyers, feedback from distributors and a thorough look at the competition. It is best done before engineering freezes the design.

seccions.titol: What the analysis has to answer before launch
seccions.text:
The analysis has to lead to a decision. It should say which customers will buy the equipment, for which modality, such as monoclonal antibodies, vaccines, cell therapy or microbial fermentation, and at what scale, lab, pilot or production. It should also say what those customers use today and why they would switch.
Do it before engineering freezes the design, while you can still change volumes, connections or the control software. If you do it afterwards, it will only justify what has already been built. Give it a clear goal from the start, such as deciding whether the equipment goes ahead, for which customer and with what message.

seccions.titol: Public data gives you the first map
seccions.text:
Start with industry reports. The AseBio Report 2025, with 2024 data, counts 1,119 biotech companies in Spain. Catalonia is home to 23.32 percent of them and generates 43.05 percent of revenue, followed by Madrid with 32.84 percent. If your customer is a Spanish biotech, most of the sector's revenue sits in these two regions.
Check what each report counts. AseBio separates these 1,119 biotech companies from the 4,465 companies with some biotech activity. Biocat's 2025 BioRegion of Catalonia Report lists 1,650 companies in Catalonia because it covers the entire life sciences and healthcare sector. Mix definitions and your market size will come out inflated.

seccions.titol: A few large accounts and many small buyers
seccions.text:
Revenue is highly concentrated. According to AseBio, large companies with more than 250 employees account for 58.7 percent of biotech revenue, and micro companies for just 1.9 percent. For production-scale equipment, the real market is a small number of accounts, worked one by one with sales and marketing in step.
For lab equipment it is the other way round. There are many startups, spin-offs and research groups, each with a small budget, and SEO, campaigns, distributors and demos tend to work better there. You can also see where they work, since 55.5 percent of biotech companies focus on human health and 32.6 percent on food.
