Your booth message should say in one sentence what you make, for which process and at what scale, and it has to read from the aisle. A bioprocess buyer wants to know at a glance whether you work for mAbs, vaccines or cell and gene therapy, whether you build single-use or stainless steel systems and how many litres you go up to.
Bring the equipment people can touch and show the rest on screen. A benchtop bioreactor or a lab-scale TFF system can be shipped and run on the booth. Pilot and production scales are easier to explain with renders, a process animation or a 3D configurator, which then keep working for the website and the sales team.

seccions.titol: What an ACHEMA 2027 exhibitor pays and when
seccions.text:
ACHEMA 2027 space costs from €378 to €529.20 per square metre excluding VAT, depending on the open sides, and start-ups and academic research institutions pay €239. The minimum stand is 12 square metres, or 18 for stands away from the hall walls with two or more open sides. Stand build and services are charged separately.
The space is paid in three instalments. First €94 per square metre when you apply. Then 65% of the balance, dated 15 September 2026, plus the visitor flat rate, which is €220 for 12 square metres. Finally the remaining 35% on 15 February 2027, together with the €495 media package. If you apply now, ask how the second instalment will be invoiced.
CPHI Frankfurt does not publish prices. For 2027 the organiser offers three formats. The Basic Package, formerly space only, where you build the stand yourself, the Modular Stand Design with graphics and a single point of contact, and the Shell Stand, which it calls its most affordable option and which has a later purchase deadline. You get the price through the booking form.

faqs.q: When is ACHEMA 2027?
faqs.a: ACHEMA 2027 takes place from 14 to 18 June 2027 in Frankfurt am Main, Germany. There is no application deadline, but space is let on availability. The online application is binding, and since 1 September 2026 cancelling already costs 50% of the agreed fees, so check the budget before you apply.

faqs.q: Can I exhibit at ACHEMA with a small stand?
faqs.a: Yes. The minimum stand size is 12 square metres, and ACHEMA offers all-in-one stand packages, an area for first-time exhibitors and a start-up area. You can also join a partner's or distributor's stand as a co-exhibitor, with a fee of 1,645 euros per company plus VAT.

faqs.q: How do I know whether ACHEMA or CPHI suits me better?
faqs.a: Look at who buys your equipment. If it is engineering firms, process plants and development labs, ACHEMA is the closer fit. If it is pharma companies and CDMOs sourcing suppliers across the chain, CPHI has bioproduction and machinery zones. A careful option is to exhibit at one and visit the other before deciding on the next cycle.

faqs.q: When is CPHI Frankfurt 2027?
faqs.a: CPHI Frankfurt 2027 takes place from 9 to 11 November 2027 at Messe Frankfurt. It covers the whole pharma supply chain, with bioproduction and machinery zones, and for 2027 it announces a new lab and analytical equipment zone. Stand prices are not public, so you request them through the organiser's booking form.

bio-proveidors-respostes-ia.intro: AI answers in Google and ChatGPT are built from pages these systems can crawl and index, and they link to the ones they use. To show up when a buyer looks for bioprocess suppliers, your site has to be indexable, each application needs its own page with data in plain text, and your company has to appear with the same details at trade shows, in directories and in trade media. Then you test the real questions.

seccions.titol: How an AI answer is put together when someone looks for suppliers
seccions.text:
Google explains that AI Overviews and AI Mode may use a technique it calls query fan-out. The system runs several related searches across subtopics and data sources and uses the results to write the answer, with links to the pages that support it. If a buyer asks for single-use bioreactors for cell therapy, the answer can draw on manufacturer sites, directories and articles.
To appear as a supporting link, Google only requires the page to be indexed and eligible to show in Search with a snippet. There are no extra requirements. For ChatGPT, OpenAI says sites that block its OAI-SearchBot crawler will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers, although they can still appear as navigational links.

seccions.titol: One page per application, with the data written as text
seccions.text:
Buyers rarely type just «bioreactor». They ask about a volume, an application and a type of system. Monoclonal antibodies, vaccines, cell and gene therapy or precision fermentation each deserve their own page, with scales, materials, control options, single-use or stainless steel and the documentation you supply. Google recommends making important content available as text, not only in a PDF or an image.
Google also warns against the opposite. Creating pages for every search variation just to show up in AI answers breaks its scaled content abuse policy. Its guide to generative AI search asks for original content based on first-hand experience. For an equipment maker that means test data, scale-up cases and application notes built from your own work.

seccions.titol: Company details that are clear and consistent everywhere
seccions.text:
An AI system has to understand who you are before it cites you. Your company page should state in text what you make, for which applications, across which volume range, where you manufacture and which markets you sell into. The same name and details should appear on LinkedIn, Google Business Profile, industry directories and trade show exhibitor listings.
Google recommends keeping Merchant Center and Business Profile information up to date and making sure structured data matches the visible text on the page. If one place says you build systems up to 500 litres and another says 1,000, the answer may pick the wrong figure.

seccions.titol: Where you should be mentioned beyond your own website
seccions.text: Because answers draw on several sources, your website alone is not enough. Exhibitor lists at shows such as ACHEMA or BioSpain, member pages of industry associations and articles in trade media all describe who does what. If you appear there with a clear description that matches your website, AI systems have more than one place to find you.

seccions.titol: How to test the questions a buyer would really ask
seccions.text:
Write the questions the way a buyer would, not the way your marketing team would. Ask them in ChatGPT, Google AI Mode and other assistants without signing in, and note who appears and which sources are cited. Repeat it every month with the same questions, because the answers change.
In Search Console, traffic from AI Overviews and AI Mode is counted in the Performance report under the Web search type. Also check that robots.txt and your CDN let Googlebot and OAI-SearchBot through. We run this check before touching any copy.

faqs.q: Do I need an llms.txt file or special markup to appear in Google's AI features?
faqs.a: For Google, no. Its documentation says you do not need new machine-readable files, AI text files or special markup, and there is no special schema.org structured data for this. Other assistants may work differently, but the foundation is the same, a page that can be crawled and indexed, with its content available as text.

faqs.q: Is GEO or AEO different from SEO?
faqs.a: Google says that optimising for generative AI search is optimising for the search experience, so it is still SEO. It also suggests reviewing third-party advice sold as AEO or GEO carefully. What changes is how you test the results, with longer questions and across several assistants rather than one ranking report.

faqs.q: If I block AI crawlers, will I disappear from ChatGPT?
faqs.a: It depends on which one you block. OpenAI separates GPTBot, which signals whether content may be used to train its models, from OAI-SearchBot, which is used for search. You can block the first and allow the second. If you block OAI-SearchBot, your site will not appear in ChatGPT search answers, although it can still show up as a navigational link.

bio-render-3d-equips-proces.intro: crida studio makes 3D renders of bioreactors, skids and lab equipment for websites, catalogues, trade shows and video, from €450 per image excluding VAT. A 3D render can show what a camera cannot reach. The inside of a bioreactor with its impeller and probes, how a single-use bag fits its holder, or a skid that has not been built yet. It also gives you publishable images when a customer's GMP site is off limits for photography. A photo, on the other hand, proves the equipment exists and shows it as it really is.

seccions.titol: A render shows the inside without opening the equipment
seccions.text:
The biggest thing a render adds is the cutaway. You can remove half of the vessel wall and show the impeller, the sparger, the pH, dissolved oxygen and temperature probes, and how the liquid moves. A photo of a stainless steel bioreactor only shows a closed vessel and a control panel.
Single-use equipment works the same way. Buyers want to see how the bag goes into the holder, where the ports, tubing and connectors sit, and what gets thrown away after each batch. An exploded view or a sequence of three images explains that better than a long paragraph on the product page.

seccions.titol: You can show a skid before it is built
seccions.text:
A lot of process equipment is built to order. While you are negotiating a TFF skid or a media preparation line, there is nothing to photograph yet. A render made from the engineering 3D model helps the customer see the footprint, where the valves go and how operators reach it for cleaning and maintenance.
There is a risk here. If the render does not match what gets delivered, questions will come up at FAT. So engineering should check every image before it is published, and the caption should say clearly whether it shows an example configuration or the final equipment.

seccions.titol: When the customer's cleanroom cannot be photographed
seccions.text:
Many GMP sites will not simply let a photographer in. Annex 1 of the EU GMP guidelines asks for only the minimum number of personnel in cleanrooms (point 7.2) and says unqualified people should not enter grade B cleanrooms or grade A in operation (point 7.5). Only materials and equipment on an approved list should be transferred into grade A and B areas (point 4.12).
On top of that, customers often do not want their facility, their process or their logo on show. A render solves both problems. The equipment can sit in a generic cleanroom, with whatever lighting and angle you need, without revealing anything the customer has not approved.

seccions.titol: Where photography still wins
seccions.text:
A photo proves things a render cannot. That the equipment exists, that there is a workshop where it is assembled, people who test it and customers who already use it. In a sector where buyers compare suppliers for months and go through quality before deciding, that proof of reality counts.
The mix that tends to work is renders to explain and photos to prove. Clean renders for the catalogue, product pages and sales decks, and real photos of the workshop, the testing and the equipment running for the company page, news and trade shows.

seccions.titol: What to have ready so the render stays accurate
seccions.text: A render of process equipment is only as accurate as the information behind it. If a drawing or a finish is missing, the 3D artist has to guess and images get redone later. Before starting, gather these materials with your engineering and product teams.

faqs.q: Can renders replace product photos in the catalogue?
faqs.a: For product pages and the catalogue, often yes, because renders give you consistent views across the range and let you show variants without building them. Even so, keep real photos of the equipment running, the workshop and the testing. Many buyers want to see them before they put a supplier on the shortlist.

faqs.q: Where does the 3D model come from if the equipment does not exist yet?
faqs.a: Usually from the CAD model engineering already uses to design the equipment. If there is none, it can be modelled from drawings, dimensions and photos of similar parts, but it needs more checking. Either way, engineering should approve the result before anything is published.

faqs.q: Can a render go into a technical proposal?
faqs.a: Yes, and it helps the buyer understand what you are offering. Label it as an illustration. What counts is the technical documentation that answers the customer's URS, with drawings and specifications. At FAT and SAT the equipment is checked against those documents.

faqs.q: Who can make 3D renders of bioreactors?
faqs.a: crida studio makes 3D renders of bioreactors, skids and lab equipment from the manufacturer's CAD, from €450 per image excluding VAT. They work for websites, catalogues, trade shows and video, especially to show the inside of the equipment or a model that hasn't been built yet. A cutaway, a full GMP suite or an animation is quoted separately.

bio-render-o-foto-sala-blanca.intro: To show equipment inside a cleanroom, a render wins when the facility belongs to a customer, the process is confidential or the system is not installed yet. Photography wins when you need to prove the equipment exists and runs, and you can often shoot it in your own workshop, during FAT or before the room goes into production. Often the best answer is a mix of both.

seccions.titol: What photographing inside a GMP cleanroom involves
seccions.text:
A photo shoot in a grade A or B area is an operation the site has to plan. EU GMP Annex 1 says unqualified personnel should not enter grade B or grade A in operation (point 7.5). If it is needed in an exceptional case, it has to follow a written procedure, under supervision, and be recorded.
Equipment matters too. Annex 1 keeps watches, make-up, jewellery, phones and other non-essential items out of clean areas (point 7.9). Anything going into grade A or B must pass through a process that does not bring in contamination, such as sterilisation or a validated transfer disinfection (point 4.11). Camera, tripod and lights must be cleanable, and the site has to agree to let them in.

seccions.titol: What ends up in the shot and what to check first
seccions.text:
In grade B, Annex 1 calls for a hood, a facemask and goggles that cover the whole face (point 7.13). In the photos, you can barely recognise anyone. That helps when the customer's staff must not appear, but it will not show your own people or put a face to your service team.
Before shooting, look at everything around the equipment. Customer logos, product or batch labels, control screens showing process data, whiteboards and other suppliers' systems. Any of these can reveal information the customer wants to protect. Every shot needs the customer's approval before it goes on the website, into the catalogue or onto a trade show stand.

seccions.titol: When a render is the better option
seccions.text:
A render covers the cases where a photo is impossible or not worth the effort. The system is not installed yet, the facility belongs to a customer who does not want it seen, or you need the same clean room across the whole range. The equipment goes into a generic cleanroom, with whatever light and angle you need, and nobody has to gown up.
It can also show things a real room cannot. For example, the system connected to the rest of the line, each grade zone marked in colour, or the path material takes through the airlock. The condition is that engineering validates the scene and the caption makes clear it is an illustration.

seccions.titol: When you need real photography
seccions.text:
A photo is proof that the equipment exists and works in a real facility. It carries weight wherever buyers look for trust, such as the company page, a case study the customer has approved or news of an installation. However good a render is, it cannot prove any of that.
You do not need to get into the customer's cleanroom to have real photos. You can shoot in your own workshop, in the test area during FAT or in your own cleanroom if you have one. You can also ask the customer whether photos are possible before the room goes into production, for example during SAT.

seccions.titol: Photography or render, criterion by criterion
seccions.text: The table sums up what usually tips the decision. Cost has no figures because it depends on too many things. For example, whether a 3D model already exists, how many views you need or how many hours of site time and customer staff a photo shoot takes.

seccions.titol: How to mix photos and renders without a visible jump
seccions.text:
Plan both at the same time. If the photo shoot and the renders use similar angles and lighting, the catalogue looks consistent even when it mixes the two. Start with the list of images you need and decide, one by one, whether each will be a photo or a render.
Every caption should say what the image is. A render, a photo in your workshop or a real installation shown with the customer's permission. In a sector where quality reviews everything, that clarity avoids awkward questions in an audit or in a meeting with the buyer.

faqs.q: Can a photographer go into a grade A or B area?
faqs.a: Only if the site allows it and organises it. EU GMP Annex 1 (point 7.5) says unqualified personnel should not enter grade B or grade A in operation, and that exceptional cases need a written procedure and supervision. So ask the customer early on and keep a fallback plan based on renders.

faqs.q: Can we publish photos of equipment installed at a customer site?
faqs.a: Only with written permission and after the customer has reviewed every image. You can propose a shot that shows nothing of their process, brand or facility. Without permission, a photo in your workshop before shipping or a render in a generic room does the same job.

faqs.q: Can a cleanroom render look fake?
faqs.a: It can if the room is too perfect or details do not add up, such as doors without an airlock, surfaces that could not be cleaned or people without the right gowning for the grade. Have someone from quality or engineering review the whole scene, not just the equipment, because buyers in this sector spot it straight away.

bio-roadshow-o-fira.intro: An international trade show gives you reach, meaning many buyers who do not know you yet within a few days. A demo roadshow gives you depth, because you take the equipment to a handful of accounts that are already interested. For a bioprocess equipment maker the answer is usually a mixed calendar, with one major show as the anchor and roadshow stops before and after.

seccions.titol: Trade shows give reach, roadshows give depth
seccions.text:
The main difference is who is standing in front of you. A show brings a stream of people you do not know, with short and noisy conversations. On a roadshow you pick the list, travel to the customer's city, a distributor's lab or the customer's own site, and the demo can take as long as it needs.
So the useful question is where your accounts are in the buying process. If you still need to find them, go to the show. If you already know them and they are torn between two suppliers, take the roadshow. A small sales team cannot do everything, and the wrong choice also costs your people's time.

seccions.titol: What an international show like ACHEMA gives you
seccions.text:
A major show packs buyers from many countries into a few days. According to the official figures, ACHEMA 2024 drew 106,001 participants and 2,842 exhibitors from 56 countries, and for 52 percent of visitors it is the only trade show they attend. The next edition runs from 14 to 18 June 2027 in Frankfurt.
Look at where the audience comes from as well. At ACHEMA 2024, 51.1 percent of participants came from Germany and only 7.4 percent from Southern Europe. If your main market is Germany, it fits. If you are looking for customers in Spain, a local show or a roadshow may pay off better.

seccions.titol: Trade show or roadshow, criterion by criterion
seccions.text: The table sums up what changes for an equipment maker. Cost per useful meeting varies a lot from case to case, so work it out with your own numbers, adding up booth, travel, equipment shipping and staff hours, then dividing by the meetings that turned into real opportunities.

seccions.titol: A yearly calendar that combines both
seccions.text:
A practical option is to make one major show the anchor and build the roadshow around it. Before the show, a few stops to invite key accounts to the booth. Afterwards, stops in the markets that produced the most opportunities, often with the local distributor, who knows the customers and can lend you a room or a lab.
Build one kit that serves everything, with the demo unit, the booth loop video, data sheets in English and in the local language and a twenty-minute demo script. And tag the source of every contact in your CRM, so after a year you can compare what each format actually brought in.

faqs.q: What equipment can we take on a roadshow?
faqs.a: Anything that fits in a van and can be set up in a few hours, such as lab bioreactors, benchtop TFF systems, single-use bags and assemblies or the control software on a screen. For production scale, use a 3D configurator, a process animation or a visit to a reference site if the customer allows it.

faqs.q: Can a roadshow replace a trade show?
faqs.a: Rarely in full. A roadshow needs a list of accounts to visit, and much of that list is built at trade shows, through SEO, campaigns and distributors. If you skip a show one year, make up for it with extra effort to find new names, or the roadshow will run out of people to visit.

faqs.q: How do we work out cost per meeting for each format?
faqs.a: Add up every cost of the format, including booth or meeting rooms, travel, equipment shipping and people's hours, and divide it by the meetings that produced a real opportunity in the CRM. Compare formats on the same basis and over a full year, because equipment sales take months to close.

faqs.q: Should we run the roadshow with our distributors?
faqs.a: In countries where you sell through distributors, yes. They know the customers, can fill the room and will handle the follow-up. Prepare the content and the demo, let the distributor send the invitations and agree beforehand who calls each attendee and by when.

bio-seguiment-contactes-fira.intro: Get leads into the CRM within the first 48 hours, segment them by project stage and scale, and send a first email that refers to the demo they saw. Ask for permission to send commercial information right there on the booth. The more days go by, the less the contact remembers the conversation and the more your email looks like everyone else's.

seccions.titol: Why follow-up has to happen the same week
seccions.text:
AUMA, the German trade fair industry association, says the success of a show depends on how quickly and specifically leads are followed up. It also notes that a visitor can hold up to 13 meetings in a single day. Your booth is one of those conversations, and the email you send afterwards competes with all the others.
In bioprocessing, the sales cycle is also long and several people have a say. If the first follow-up arrives late or reads like a template, your contact is unlikely to forward it to quality, engineering or procurement. Good follow-up gives them something useful to pass on to the rest of their team.

seccions.titol: What to decide before you go to the show
seccions.text:
AUMA recommends defining lead criteria before the show and using one standard capture process on the booth. In practice that means a short form in the app or on a tablet, with the same fields for every conversation and a clear checkbox for permission to send information.
Article 13(1) of the GDPR says people must be informed at the moment their data is collected. Article 7(1) says that when processing is based on consent, you must be able to demonstrate that it was given. That is why the checkbox and the privacy notice belong in the booth form.

seccions.titol: The first 48 hours, from badge scanner to CRM
seccions.text:
A badge scan gives you a name and a company, but not the context. The context is in the booth notes. On the first day after the show, export the scans and the notes, merge them, remove duplicates and assign each contact to a salesperson or a distributor.
Then segment them. A production manager with a pilot plant project this year cannot get the same email as a researcher who was looking at lab equipment. Three tags, for stage, scale and contact type, are enough to run different follow-ups without writing a hundred emails by hand.

seccions.titol: A follow-up email about what they saw on the booth
seccions.text:
The first email should bring the conversation back. Mention the demo or the scale they saw, attach the material that fits, such as the bioreactor datasheet, the animation video or a render at their scale, and suggest a concrete next step, such as a call with the application engineer. It works better if it comes from the person they spoke to.
In Spain, Article 21(1) of the LSSI bans commercial emails that the recipient has not requested or expressly authorised beforehand. Article 21(2) exempts cases with a prior contractual relationship, provided the contact details were obtained lawfully and the email is about the company's own products or services similar to those the customer originally bought.
In every case, the same article requires a simple, free procedure to object to the use of their data for promotional purposes, both when it is collected and in every commercial communication. Article 21(4) of the GDPR adds that the right to object must be explicitly brought to the person's attention at the latest at the time of the first communication. Other countries have their own rules, so check before each campaign.

faqs.q: Can I send marketing emails to every badge I scanned at the show?
faqs.a: In Spain, Article 21 of the LSSI only allows commercial emails if the person requested or expressly authorised them beforehand, or if there is a prior contractual relationship and the email is about products or services similar to those already bought. That is why your booth form should collect permission clearly and keep a record of it. Rules differ by country, so if in doubt, ask your data protection adviser.

faqs.q: When should I send the first email after a trade show?
faqs.a: Within the same week, ideally in the first 48 hours. The contact still remembers the conversation and the demo they saw. If the show ends on a Friday, have the leads in the CRM that weekend or first thing on Monday.

faqs.q: What do I do with contacts who are not potential customers?
faqs.a: Tag them separately and keep them out of the sales sequence. Students, suppliers, competitors or job candidates can be useful for other things, such as hiring or market insight, but if they get the same emails as a buyer they pollute your data and waste your sales team's time.

bio-seo-fabricant-equips.intro: Short searches like «bioreactor» are the most contested. A mid-sized lab and bioprocess equipment manufacturer has better odds with searches that combine application, scale and equipment type. SEO starts with a keyword map by application and scale, continues with pages an engineer would bookmark, and is measured with Search Console queries and the quote requests that follow.

seccions.titol: What equipment buyers actually type into Google
seccions.text:
People buying equipment rarely type just the equipment name. They type the application, the scale and a condition or two, such as «50 L single-use bioreactor for cell culture» or «TFF system to concentrate antibodies at pilot scale». These searches have little volume, but whoever runs them often has a project on the table already.
Google's SEO starter guide points the same way. It says people who know a topic well use different words from newcomers, and that it pays to write with those differences in mind. It also says you do not need to anticipate every variation, because its systems understand how a page relates to many queries.

seccions.titol: A keyword map by application and scale, not by model
seccions.text:
Only people who already know you search for model names. To reach new buyers, lay your keywords out on a grid. One axis holds applications, such as monoclonal antibodies, vaccines, cell and gene therapy or precision fermentation. The other holds scales, from the lab to pilot plant and GMP production. Every cell with real demand deserves its own page.
The data to fill the grid comes from three places. The queries already bringing visits in Search Console, the questions your sales team gets by email and at trade shows, and the wording customers use in their user requirement specifications, or URS. Anything that shows up nowhere does not need a page of its own.

seccions.titol: The pages an engineer bookmarks
seccions.text:
Some pages a process engineer saves and keeps coming back to. Application notes with test data, scale-up tables with working volumes, material compatibility lists, or a clear account of what the FAT, SAT, IQ and OQ documentation covers. They are useful before and after the purchase, which is why they belong on a manufacturer's website.
Google asks for people-first content with original information and first-hand expertise, the kind that comes from actually using a product. A manufacturer has it, because it designs, builds and tests the equipment. Put that data in the page text and keep the PDF as a download, so it can be read without opening a file.

seccions.titol: How to structure the site so Google understands it
seccions.text:
Google recommends descriptive URLs and explains that, on sites with thousands of URLs, grouping topics in directories helps it learn how often each part changes. For a manufacturer, one directory for applications and another for product ranges or scales makes sense. It also notes that keywords in the domain or URL alone have hardly any effect, and that it ignores the meta keywords tag.
For equipment, Google offers two kinds of product structured data. Product snippets are for pages where people cannot buy directly, which is the usual case for equipment sold on quotation. Merchant listings are for pages where customers can buy from you, such as an online shop for consumables.

seccions.titol: How to tell whether SEO brings in buyers
seccions.text:
The Search Console Performance report shows the queries that bring clicks, the pages that receive them and the countries they come from. Filter it by the terms for each application and scale and check whether long queries are growing. Google warns that some changes show up in hours and others take months, and suggests waiting a few weeks before judging them.
Visits do not buy equipment, though. Record on the website and in your CRM which page each quote request comes from. That tells you which applications bring real projects and where you need to write more. We always start with this review before proposing new pages.

faqs.q: How long does SEO take to show results for an equipment manufacturer?
faqs.a: Google says some changes take effect within hours and others can take several months, and it suggests waiting a few weeks before assessing the impact. Equipment makers also have a long buying cycle on top of that. So it makes sense to watch queries and visits to application pages first, and then the quote requests those pages generate.

faqs.q: Do we need an English website if we sell outside Spain?
faqs.a: If you sell abroad, almost certainly yes, because much of the sector's vocabulary is in English. If you have customers or distributors in Germany or the Nordics, consider German or other languages as well. Each language needs its own pages, reviewed by someone who knows the process vocabulary, rather than an unreviewed machine translation.

bio-single-use-acer-inox-web.intro: The best way to explain single-use vs stainless steel on your website is a page that helps buyers decide on clear criteria. It should compare batch size, product changeovers, CIP and SIP cleaning, extractables and leachables, supply and cost. A buyer who sees the strengths and limits of each option trusts the company that explains them, even if they end up choosing the other one.

seccions.titol: Why a decision page persuades better than a brochure
seccions.text:
Anyone buying a bioreactor or a TFF system already knows both technologies. They want to know which one fits their process, their scale and their production plan. If your website only lists the benefits of one option, the process development team reads it as advertising and looks for a comparison elsewhere.
A decision page explains when each technology fits and when it does not, and ends with an offer to talk through the specific case. It works even if you only make one of the two, because it brings you enquiries from people who already know your option is the right one for them.

seccions.titol: The criteria that tip the decision
seccions.text: The comparison should follow the order in which buyers think. Batch size and number of products come first, then cleaning and validation, and finally supply and cost. The table sums up how each criterion can be presented without declaring a winner.

seccions.titol: What EU GMP Annex 1 says about single-use systems
seccions.text:
Annex 1 of the EU GMP guidelines covers the manufacture of sterile medicinal products, and since its 2022 revision points 8.131 to 8.139 deal with single-use systems. They list risks the drug manufacturer must assess, such as interaction between the product and the contact material, extractables and leachables, fragility compared with fixed systems, leaks and particles.
Point 8.134 says that assessing the suppliers of these systems is critical when selecting them. So your single-use page should answer these questions before the quality team asks them. These are the points worth having published or ready to send.

seccions.titol: How to make the case for stainless steel without sounding dated
seccions.text:
Stainless steel is still the logical choice for many high-volume projects with few product changes. The investment is spread over many batches and the plant depends less on a steady supply of consumables. Your website should make that case with process examples rather than presenting it as the way things have always been done.
Buyers want to see how cleaning is handled. Point 10.1 of Annex 15 of the EU GMP guidelines requires cleaning validation for all product contact equipment. A good page explains the hygienic design, how CIP and SIP work and which documents you provide to validate cleaning at the customer's site.

seccions.titol: How to present single-use without overpromising
seccions.text:
Cleaning is one of the strongest arguments for single-use. In a BioPlan Associates survey published in BioProcess International in 2009, 88% of biopharmaceutical production decision makers said eliminating cleaning was an important or very important reason to adopt it. Lower cross-contamination risk and getting a facility running sooner came close behind.
Your page should build on these reasons without exaggerating. Promises such as zero contamination risk clash with Annex 1, which asks manufacturers to assess risks like leaks and particles. It works better to explain how you reduce those risks and how you secure the supply of bags and connectors.

seccions.titol: If you make both technologies, talk about hybrid facilities
seccions.text:
Many facilities combine both options. They may run stainless steel production bioreactors and use single-use for media and buffer preparation or product storage. If you make both, your website can help customers plan that combination instead of showing them two separate catalogues.
TECNIC, for example, presents single-use and reusable versions of its bioreactors and TFF systems on its website, along with ancillary equipment such as a CIP system. David Monje, founder of crida studio, ran its marketing for three and a half years. A dual offer like this is the natural starting point for a decision page.

faqs.q: If we only make single-use equipment, should we mention stainless steel?
faqs.a: Yes, briefly and without running it down. Buyers will make the comparison anyway, and if they find it on your website they will trust you more. Explaining when stainless steel is the better fit also filters enquiries, because the people who contact you already know their project suits single-use.

faqs.q: Should we publish our extractables and leachables data?
faqs.a: You do not need to publish full reports, but you should explain which studies you have, for which components and how to request them. Point 8.136 of Annex 1 calls for these profiles to be evaluated, and supplier data helps the drug manufacturer do it. If people have to request the data, keep the form short and reply quickly.

faqs.q: How do we know if the decision page is working?
faqs.a: Track how many enquiries come from that page and which technology they ask about. If your form includes fields such as batch size or number of products, you will see which projects it brings in. It also helps to ask your sales team whether buyers arrive better informed at the first meeting.

bio-traduccio-tecnica-ia.intro: Yes, as long as AI produces the draft and not the final version. Start with a glossary of approved terms for each language, then translate with AI, then have a native-speaking engineer who knows the process review it. Instruction manuals are a separate case, because the EU Machinery Regulation, which applies from 20 January 2027, requires the language set by each Member State.

seccions.titol: Where AI helps and where the risk is
seccions.text:
AI translates fast and, given enough context, keeps a consistent tone across long texts. For a product page, an application note or a newsletter, it can produce a first draft in minutes. The risk sits in technical terms, units, decimals and safety warnings, which is exactly where a mistake has consequences.
Take one example. If the glossary does not say how to translate working volume, the output can confuse a bioreactor's working volume with its total volume. For a process engineer comparing 50 and 200-litre systems, that difference changes the purchase. That is why the order is glossary, draft and review, never the other way round.

seccions.titol: Glossary first, translation second
seccions.text: The glossary is a table listing each technical term in the reference language with its approved translation in every target language. Engineering should sign it off and, ideally, so should the local distributor, who knows how customers actually talk. It then goes into the AI tool with every job, so the same terms are used every time.

seccions.titol: How much control each type of content needs
seccions.text: Not all content carries the same risk. A newsletter with an awkward phrase can be fixed in the next issue, but a badly translated safety instruction can hurt someone. The table sorts the usual content of a bioprocess equipment manufacturer by the level of control it needs before publication.

seccions.titol: Why manuals fall under the Machinery Regulation
seccions.text:
For equipment that counts as machinery, Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 applies from 20 January 2027. Article 10(7) requires instructions for use, safety information and the information in Annex III to be in a language easily understood by users, as determined by the Member State, and to be clear, understandable and legible. Article 15 requires distributors to check this before they sell.
The same article allows instructions in digital form. In that case they must be printable and downloadable, stay online for the expected lifetime of the equipment and for at least ten years after it is placed on the market, and if the customer asks for paper at the time of purchase, it must be provided free of charge within one month.
Section 1.7.4 of Annex III makes one exception. Maintenance instructions for specialised personnel authorised by the manufacturer may be supplied in just one official EU language that those staff understand. The rest has to be in the language set by each Member State where the equipment is sold. So it makes sense to keep the glossary and translations under version control, just like the equipment itself.

seccions.titol: What Google makes of an AI-translated website
seccions.text:
Google looks at the value of a page more than the tool used to make it. Its policy on scaled content abuse targets pages created mainly to manipulate rankings that offer little or no value to users, no matter how they were created. Its examples include using generative AI to produce many pages without adding value, and translating scraped content from other sites automatically.
In practice, a site translated with AI and properly reviewed, with one page per language and correct hreflang, is just a normal multilingual website. A site with hundreds of pages machine-translated in one go and never checked is much closer to what Google describes as abuse, and a native-speaking customer will notice by the first sentence.

faqs.q: Which AI tool is best for translating technical documents?
faqs.a: Whichever lets you work with a glossary, give context and keep the document's formatting. The workflow matters more than the tool. Run a test with one product page and one application note, have a native engineer review both and compare the errors. Confidential material such as customer URS documents should not go into tools that do not guarantee confidentiality in their contract.

faqs.q: Can we translate the instruction manual with AI?
faqs.a: The regulation does not say which tool to use. It says the result must be in the language set by each Member State and be clear, understandable and legible, and the manufacturer is accountable for it. If AI produces the draft, the review must be complete and done by someone who masters both the language and the equipment.

faqs.q: Do datasheets need translating too?
faqs.a: If they are part of how you sell in that market, yes. Engineers compare specifications and want them in their own language or, at the very least, in English. AI saves a lot of time here because the text is short and repetitive, but every figure, every unit and the decimal separator need checking, since they vary from country to country.

bio-triar-mercat-exportacio.intro: Pick the market where your equipment solves a clear problem and where you can provide service, rather than the biggest one on the map. Germany and Scandinavia work to European GMP rules and are close by, while Asia calls for more adaptation and a strong local partner. Score each option on five criteria with public data before you spend on trade shows and translation.

seccions.titol: The best market is where you can win and provide service
seccions.text:
Before looking at which country buys the most bioreactors, ask where you have the best chance of winning. Process equipment is not sold on a good datasheet alone. Customers want installation, qualification support, spare parts and someone who picks up the phone during working hours. If you cannot guarantee that in a country, that country is not ready for you yet.
That is why it pays to compare markets on concrete criteria and data you can check. The most useful are the enquiries already coming in from each country, distributor interest, the rules your customers follow and the trade show calendar. That way the decision no longer rests only on the sales director's instinct.

seccions.titol: Five criteria to score each market
seccions.text: Score each country from 1 to 5 on each criterion and add it up. It is not an exact science, but it makes the team write down why it is choosing a market and helps explain the decision to management and sales. Do it with someone from product and someone from engineering, who spot risks marketing does not see.

seccions.titol: The regulatory route changes the marketing work
seccions.text:
Germany, Denmark, Sweden and Finland are in the EU, and their customers work to EU GMP just as in Spain. The documentation you already use, such as URS responses, FAT and SAT protocols and IQ, OQ and PQ support, largely still works. What changes is the language and the references.
In Asia each country has its own authority. The PIC/S list, the cooperation scheme between GMP inspectorates, gives you a first picture. It includes, for example, Japan, Korea, Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Hong Kong and Chinese Taipei, but not mainland China or India. The further a market sits from that framework, the more adaptation of documents and messaging you should plan for.

seccions.titol: Scandinavia, Germany or Asia, criterion by criterion
seccions.text: The table sums up what usually changes between the three options for a Spanish bioprocess equipment maker. The cells are a guide. What decides is how each criterion scores with your own data, above all the enquiries you already receive and the distributors showing interest.

seccions.titol: The 2027 trade show calendar forces a choice
seccions.text:
The dates already published make it hard. ACHEMA runs from 14 to 18 June 2027 in Frankfurt and CPHI & PMEC China from 16 to 18 June 2027 in Shanghai. With a small sales team you cannot be in both places, so decide early who goes to which show or which one you skip.
For Scandinavia, ACHEMA may not be enough. At the 2024 edition only 3.4 percent of participants came from Northern Europe. Nordic Life Science Days, on 29 and 30 September 2027 in Copenhagen, is a partnering event with startups, pharma and investors, useful for getting to know the Nordic ecosystem.

faqs.q: How many new markets can I open at once?
faqs.a: It depends on your team and budget, but for an industrial SME one market at a time is usually sensible, or two if they share a language and rules. Opening more means more translation, more travel and more distributors to look after, and in the end follow-up gets thin everywhere.

faqs.q: Do I need my website in each Nordic language?
faqs.a: To start with, try a strong English version and ask your distributor and first customers what is missing. Then translate the pieces used most, such as datasheets and manuals, into the language they ask for. Also check what each country requires for the documentation that ships with the equipment.

faqs.q: What public data can I use to compare markets?
faqs.a: Exhibitor lists and official trade show figures, the list of PIC/S participating authorities, reports from industry associations and public agencies, and news of plant investments. Combine them with your Search Console and CRM data, which tell you where people are already looking for you.

faqs.q: Is Asia worth it for an SME?
faqs.a: It can be if your product fits and you have a strong local partner who can install, train and provide service. Without that partner, distance and time difference make it hard to look after a GMP customer properly. Start with a single country, with very complete English material, and review the translation your distributor produces.

bio-trobar-distribuidors.intro: Good lab equipment distributors turn up in trade show exhibitor lists, on the websites of manufacturers selling complementary products and through public export agencies such as ICEX and ACCIÓ. Finding names is the easy part. The hard part is choosing the one whose portfolio fits your equipment and who can install it and support qualification.

seccions.titol: Where to find the first names
seccions.text:
Start with industry trade shows. At ACHEMA 2024, 2,842 companies from 56 countries exhibited. Filter the exhibitor list by the country you are interested in and look for distributors and manufacturers with their own network, especially those showing equipment that complements yours, such as analytics, chromatography or cleanrooms.
The second source is manufacturers selling complementary products that do not compete with you. Many publish their distributors by country on their website, and those distributors already call on the labs and plants you want to reach. LinkedIn helps you see who works there, what background their technical staff have and which customers they serve.

seccions.titol: Export agencies such as ICEX and ACCIÓ can open doors
seccions.text:
Public export agencies do this work every day. ICEX, Spain's trade and investment agency, says its speciality is putting companies in touch with importers, distributors, investors and technology partners. ACCIÓ, the Catalan government's business agency, has 40 offices abroad that help Catalan companies do business in more than 100 countries.
Ask the office in your target country whether they can draw up a list of potential distributors or a meeting schedule. Go in prepared, with an English datasheet for the equipment, the customer profile you are after and the criteria you will use to choose. The more specific you are, the better the names they will suggest.

seccions.titol: Check that their portfolio fits your equipment
seccions.text: A good distributor sells products that complement yours and visits the customers you want. If they already carry a direct competitor, your equipment may end up as their second choice. If they only sell consumables to hospitals, they may never reach process development labs or GMP plants. Ask these questions at the first meeting.

seccions.titol: The distribution contract shapes your marketing too
seccions.text:
In the EU, many distribution agreements can rely on Regulation (EU) 2022/720, which runs until 31 May 2034. Under Article 3, they only qualify if the supplier's share of the market where it sells does not exceed 30 percent, and the distributor's share of the market where it buys does not exceed 30 percent either.
Within that framework, Article 4(b) allows you to restrict an exclusive distributor's active sales into territories you have kept for yourself or given exclusively to another distributor. Passive sales, the ones that answer unsolicited requests from customers, generally cannot be restricted. That is why it pays to agree in writing who runs campaigns in each country.
Article 1 counts as active sales, among other things, search engine advertising aimed at customers in particular territories, a website with a country domain, or languages that are not the ones commonly used where the distributor is based. And under Article 4(e), preventing the effective use of the internet to sell removes the exemption. This is a general reading of the text, so have a lawyer review the contract.

seccions.titol: How to get started with a new distributor
seccions.text:
The first months set the tone. Run technical and sales training, give them translated material, agree a plan with the accounts you will target first and decide how you will pass leads to each other. A shared CRM or partner portal stops enquiries that come through your website from getting lost.
Track a few things and review them every quarter, such as open opportunities, demos run and quotes sent. If nothing moves after a reasonable time, talk about it openly. Often the problem is material or training, and it can be fixed before you change distributor.

faqs.q: One exclusive distributor or several?
faqs.a: For bioprocess equipment, which needs installation and service, one distributor per territory who invests in training and demos usually works better. In return, set clear targets and a trial period. Before signing, check with a lawyer how the exclusivity fits Regulation (EU) 2022/720.

faqs.q: How do I know if a distributor already sells a competitor?
faqs.a: Look at their website and catalogues, the brands they show at trade shows and their LinkedIn posts. And ask them directly at the first meeting. A serious distributor will tell you and explain how they keep the two lines apart. If they will not say, you already have your answer.

faqs.q: What does a new distributor need to start selling?
faqs.a: Datasheets and presentations in their language, renders and videos of the equipment, use cases, a demo guide and answers to the most common objections. Also technical training and a clear channel for asking for help. Without that material, each distributor improvises their own pitch and the brand gets diluted.

faqs.q: Can I run Google Ads in my distributor's country?
faqs.a: You can, but agree it in writing. If you have granted exclusivity, running campaigns there can compete with them and cause friction. A common approach is for you to handle the brand and website, route enquiries from their territory straight to them, and let them run local campaigns that follow your brand rules.

bio-urs-fat-sat-contingut.intro: Bioprocess equipment buyers have to write a URS, plan FAT and SAT and qualify the system through IQ, OQ and PQ. A manufacturer that helps with these documents before the sale takes on work the buyer already has to do. A URS checklist, a FAT and SAT outline or the index of your qualification pack all make useful content, as long as engineering reviews them before they go live.

seccions.titol: Why qualification is a strong sales topic
seccions.text:
Annex 15 of the EU GMP guidelines says the URS should be a point of reference throughout the validation life cycle (point 3.2). It also says that, before installation, equipment should be confirmed to meet the URS at the vendor site where applicable (point 3.5), and that FAT may be supplemented by a SAT once the equipment reaches the plant (point 3.7). Buyers need the manufacturer at every step.
That is why content explaining how you handle these steps answers a real concern. ISPE publishes a reference guide on commissioning and qualification, released in June 2019, with best practices for URS, design review, DQ and acceptance. Your customer's quality team knows the framework. What they want to know is how you will work within it.

seccions.titol: A checklist to help buyers prepare their URS
seccions.text:
The customer writes the URS, but often does not know where to start with a new type of system. A downloadable checklist helps them cover everything and gets them thinking about the questions your team answers well. It is one of the few pieces where asking for contact details makes sense, because whoever downloads it has a project in view.
It has to be neutral. If the checklist only leads to your own system's features, buyers notice and stop using it. It should still be useful even if they end up buying from someone else or decide to wait another year.

seccions.titol: A FAT and SAT outline buyers can read before they buy
seccions.text:
A page explaining how you run FAT answers questions that would otherwise come up late. Which tests happen at the factory, which documents the customer receives, who can attend and what is tested again at the plant during SAT. If each step has a sample document, the buyer can pass it to quality before deciding.
Annex 15 (point 3.6) says that, where appropriate and justified, documentation review and some tests performed at FAT need not be repeated at IQ or OQ, if it can be shown that transport and installation do not affect functionality. Explaining how you document this is a strong argument, as long as you never promise what the customer's quality team will accept.

seccions.titol: What goes into your qualification support pack
seccions.text:
According to Annex 15 (point 3.9), IQ includes, among other things, checking the installation against drawings, collecting the supplier's operating and maintenance instructions, calibrating instruments and verifying materials of construction. OQ tests upper and lower operating limits and worst-case conditions (point 3.11). Much of that documentation comes from the equipment manufacturer.
Publishing the index of your pack, with one sample page from each document, shows buyers what they will receive without giving away anything confidential. PQ depends on the customer's process and is carried out by them. Your content can explain how you support it, but should not present it as your own work.

seccions.titol: Where to use this content so it helps sales
seccions.text: Each piece has its place. The FAT and SAT outline and the qualification pack index go on your website, ungated and close to each product page. The URS checklist sits behind a form with automated follow-up. All of it also works in proposals, at trade shows and in a webinar with your engineers.

faqs.q: Are we giving engineering work away for free?
faqs.a: Not if the content stays general. A URS checklist or a FAT outline explains how you work, it does not solve the customer's project. Your response to their URS, specific protocols and data on their system stay within the sales process, under NDA if needed.

faqs.q: Can we say our system is GMP compliant?
faqs.a: Better not to put it that way. GMP and Annex 15 are addressed to medicine manufacturers, who qualify the equipment in their own plant. The equipment manufacturer supports them with design, documentation and testing. Your content should explain that support with concrete facts and avoid claims that depend on the customer.

faqs.q: Which document should we create first?
faqs.a: The one that answers the question you hear most. If every proposal ends with the same FAT questions, start with the FAT and SAT outline. If projects arrive without a clear URS, build the checklist. Ask your sales reps and application engineers which questions they answer most often and decide from there.

bio-vendre-equips-alemanya.intro: To sell bioprocess equipment in Germany you need four things in place before any campaign. A website and datasheets in German, documentation as complete as the local manufacturers offer, references the buyer can check, and a calendar built around ACHEMA. German buyers have suppliers close at hand, so your job is to take away the risk of buying from a manufacturer abroad.

seccions.titol: In Germany you compete with manufacturers playing at home
seccions.text:
German buyers have plenty of manufacturers nearby. At ACHEMA 2024, the big process industry show in Frankfurt, 2,842 companies from 56 countries exhibited, and 36.7 percent of them were German. Germany alone had more exhibitors than the rest of Europe put together.
So a German buyer's question is simple. Why buy a bioreactor or a TFF system from a Spanish manufacturer when there is one much closer. Your marketing has to answer it before the first meeting, with information in their language, complete documentation and evidence that other customers already trust you.

seccions.titol: German website and datasheets, starting with the key pages
seccions.text:
An English-only website can work for a first contact with a scientist, but it often falls short once procurement, quality and production get involved. Translate into German the pages for the equipment you want to sell there, the PDF datasheets, the contact form and a company page that explains who you are, where you manufacture and who provides service.
The translation has to be technical and checked by someone who speaks German and knows the field, such as an engineer at your distributor. Put these pages in a /de/ folder with hreflang so Google shows the German version to people searching from Germany, and do your keyword research in German, because the terms are not always a literal translation of the English.

seccions.titol: Documentation persuades as much as the equipment
seccions.text:
For equipment going into GMP environments, buyers often ask to see the documentation before they talk price. They want to know how you will answer their URS, what your FAT and SAT cover and how you will support IQ, OQ and PQ qualification. If your website already shows what you deliver and how, you get closer to the level of local manufacturers.
There is a legal side too. Article 10(7) of the EU Machinery Regulation 2023/1230, which applies from 20 January 2027, says instructions for use and safety information must be in a language easily understood by users, as determined by the Member State concerned. If your equipment falls under it, confirm which language Germany requires and reuse that translation on your website.

seccions.titol: References a German buyer can actually check
seccions.text:
A reference is worth more the closer it is to the buyer. One case at a lab or plant in Germany, Austria or Switzerland usually carries more weight than several cases in Spain. If you do not have one yet, start with European customers running a similar process and describe them with concrete facts such as scale, modality and the problem that was solved.
When the customer will not let you publish their name, which is common in pharma, write an anonymous case with the type of company, the bioreactor or TFF scale and the challenge. And make it clear who provides service in Germany, with a local phone number and address if you already have a distributor or service partner.

seccions.titol: Where to start if you do not sell in Germany yet
seccions.text: You do not need to do everything in year one. Pick one or two equipment lines where you have a clear edge and prepare material only for those. Then decide whether you will sell direct, through a distributor or with a service partner, because that decides the contact number, what you show on the website and who follows up.

faqs.q: Do I need to translate my whole website into German?
faqs.a: Not at first. Start with the pages for the equipment you want to sell in Germany, the datasheets, the contact form and the company page. The rest can stay in English. Extend the translation once you see which pages get visits and enquiries from Germany, and always have the copy checked by someone who knows the field.

faqs.q: Is ACHEMA worth it without a distributor in Germany?
faqs.a: It can be, if you go with a clear goal. Besides finding customers, the show is a good place to meet potential distributors and service partners. Book meetings beforehand, bring material in German and decide afterwards which sales model fits the contacts you made.

faqs.q: What if customers will not let me publish their name?
faqs.a: Write anonymous cases. Describe the type of company, the modality, such as monoclonal antibodies or cell therapy, the equipment scale and the problem solved, without details that identify the customer. Agree in writing what you can publish and, if the customer is happy to, offer the German buyer a private call with them.

faqs.q: Do I need a .de domain to sell in Germany?
faqs.a: It is not essential. A German folder on your main domain, with correct hreflang and reviewed content, lets Google show that version to people searching from Germany. A separate domain can feel more local, but it adds maintenance and SEO work, and when you are starting out it is usually easier to keep everything on one domain.

bio-video-demo-equip.intro: You film it once, with a shot list planned for three uses. Setup and connections, control software, sampling and a bag change or cleaning, each step as a clean clip. From that footage you cut a website version with captions and its own page, a silent loop for the booth and short clips your sales team can send after every meeting.

seccions.titol: One shoot with three clear uses
seccions.text:
Before you book the day, decide who will watch each version and what they need to decide. On your website, a buyer comparing suppliers opens the video. At the booth, someone walking down the aisle sees it with no sound. After a meeting, a process engineer watches it to check one detail. Three audiences, but the footage can be the same.
That is why the script is a shot list, each shot with a clean start and end, so the clips can be recombined in different orders later. Engineering reviews it before the shoot, because a step done wrong on camera will come up in a customer meeting sooner or later.

seccions.titol: The shots a bioreactor or TFF demo cannot do without
seccions.text:
The list depends on the system, but in bioprocessing the same moments come up almost every time. These are the steps a buyer wants to see before signing, because they show how much daily work their team will have and where things could go wrong in each batch.
Shoot in landscape, but leave room at the sides. That way the same shot can be cropped to vertical or square for LinkedIn without losing what matters, and you do not need to reshoot when a new format comes along.

seccions.titol: What should stay out of shot
seccions.text:
Once a video is published you cannot take it back, and in this industry some things cannot be shown. Screens with real batch data or user names, customer logos, a customer's plant without written permission or prototype features that are not for sale yet. Filming in your own lab or workshop makes all of this much easier to control.
The video should not claim more than the system does either. A voice-over saying the system is GMP or 21 CFR Part 11 compliant creates a commitment that also depends on how the customer validates it. Show concrete features, such as the audit trail or user permissions, and leave compliance statements to the documentation.

seccions.titol: The website version, with its own page and captions
seccions.text:
Google recommends a dedicated watch page for each video if you want it to appear in video results and key moments. The page must be indexed, the video cannot be hidden behind other elements and the thumbnail needs a stable URL. Key moments can be marked with structured data or in the YouTube description, which suits a demo split into steps.
The video should not slow the page down either. According to web.dev, a good experience means the main content loads within 2.5 seconds and CLS, which measures how much the page shifts while loading, stays at 0.1 or less. Reserve space for the player and add reviewed captions, because W3C says automatic ones are not enough unless confirmed accurate.

seccions.titol: Short clips for sales follow-up
seccions.text:
After a meeting, sales should not send the long video. They should send the clip that answers the question that came up, such as the bag change, cleaning or how batch data is exported. If each step is a separate clip with a clear title and its own link, the buyer can forward it to quality or production.
We cut these clips from the same footage, with on-screen text and captions in the languages the customer sells in. Stored in a library organised by system and by step, they are easy for sales to find without asking marketing every time.

faqs.q: Can we film the demo at a customer's plant?
faqs.a: Only with their written permission and following the plant's rules. EU GMP Annex 1 (point 7.2) asks for only the minimum number of people in a cleanroom, and customers often do not want their process or facility shown. That is why it is more practical to film the demo in your own lab, workshop or showroom.

faqs.q: Video or 3D render to show the equipment?
faqs.a: They do different jobs. Video proves the system exists and shows how it is really used. A render shows the inside, a system that has not been built yet or a cleanroom that cannot be photographed. On the same product page they work well together, the render to explain what it is and the video to show how people work with it.

faqs.q: Do we need a voice-over?
faqs.a: For the website and for sales, a voice-over or well-written captions help viewers follow the steps. For the booth, everything should make sense without sound. In every case, captions should be checked by hand, because W3C points out that automatic captions are often wrong and sometimes change the meaning of what is said.

bio-video-pantalla-estand.intro: Your booth screen needs a short silent loop that reads from the aisle and says in a few seconds what you make and what problem it solves. It works best with large text, one idea per shot and 3D cutaways that show the inside of the process. Edited well, the same material later serves LinkedIn and your product page.

seccions.titol: The screen exists to stop people walking past
seccions.text:
The screen has one job, which is to make someone walking down the aisle understand what you do and stop. It does not need to cover the whole catalogue or replace your sales staff. If within a few seconds it is clear that you make single-use bioreactors that scale to production, or TFF systems for CDMOs, it has done its work.
That is why the corporate video from your website rarely works as it is. It usually has a voice-over, a slow opening and shots meant for someone sitting down. At a show, people look at you while walking, from a distance and with noise all around, and anything that does not land at first glance is lost.

seccions.titol: Design it for no sound and for reading from three metres
seccions.text:
Audio is hard to hear in an exhibition hall, so everything has to work as picture and text. Use short phrases, large type and strong contrast, and leave each line on screen long enough to be read twice. One idea per shot and no small data tables.
If someone speaks on camera, use open captions, the kind that are always displayed and cannot be turned off, as the W3C accessibility initiative describes them. Before you sign off the edit, play it on a real screen from three metres away with the volume at zero. Anything that does not make sense that way should go.

seccions.titol: How to structure the loop
seccions.text: A loop has no beginning, because everyone catches it at a different point. Each segment has to make sense on its own and the brand has to be visible the whole time, not just at the end. A structure that tends to work for bioprocess equipment looks like this.

seccions.titol: Format and file, ask before you edit
seccions.text:
Ask your stand builder for the size and orientation of every screen, the resolution, the media player and the file format it accepts. A vertical LED wall, a totem and a landscape TV each need a different edit, and reworking it on the last day rarely goes well.
Deliver the file early and test it on the actual screen. Check that the loop does not flash black when it restarts, that brightness does not blow out the whites and that text reads under the hall lighting. Bring a copy on a USB stick just in case.

seccions.titol: The same edit for LinkedIn and the product page
seccions.text:
Short social versions come straight out of the loop. For video ads, LinkedIn recommends landscape, square or vertical formats, a length of 15 to 30 seconds, putting the most impactful content in the first 10 seconds and adding subtitles. Because the loop is already built for no sound, the adaptation is quick.
On the product page, Google needs the video embedded on the page with a thumbnail at a stable URL, and recommends a dedicated watch page for each video where it makes sense, plus structured data. Below is an example of a short product piece that can work on the website, on social media and at a show.

faqs.q: How long should a booth loop video be?
faqs.a: There is no single number. What matters is that each segment makes sense on its own, because nobody watches it from start to finish. A short loop repeats more often and gives you more chances to catch someone. If the edit grows because you want to cover the whole range, split it into several loops for different screens.

faqs.q: Should the booth video have music or a voice-over?
faqs.a: In an exhibition hall it will usually go unheard. If you have an enclosed area or give presentations on the booth with a microphone, sound can work there. For the screen facing the aisle, design for silence from the start and keep music for the website or social versions.

faqs.q: 3D render or real footage of the equipment?
faqs.a: Both. Real footage of the plant, the cleanroom or the unit running builds credibility, and 3D shows the inside, the flow and the scale that a camera cannot capture. If the unit is not built yet or is too large to film well, 3D lets you have the video ready in time for the show.

faqs.q: Can we reuse the booth video on our website?
faqs.a: Yes, but make a version meant for the web. The product page can carry a slightly longer cut with subtitles or voice, a clear thumbnail and, for an important video, its own watch page so Google can show it. On LinkedIn, a short square or vertical cut works better.

bio-web-cdmo-cro.intro: Biotech and pharma sponsors often build the shortlist of CDMOs and CROs they will send an RFP to from what they find on websites, on LinkedIn and at trade shows. So your website has to state plainly which modalities you handle, at what scale and phase, the GMP status of each site and how tech transfer works. If sponsors cannot find that, they move on to the next provider.

seccions.titol: What a sponsor checks before sending you an RFP
seccions.text:
Before sending a request for proposal, the development or procurement team at a biotech draws up a first list of providers. That list often comes from what they find on websites, on LinkedIn and at trade shows. If your site only says you offer integrated development and manufacturing services, they have no reason to include you.
Simon-Kucher's CDMO Growth Report 2026, based on a survey of more than 120 CDMO and pharma leaders, finds that a differentiated value proposition is the top commercial initiative in every CDMO segment. It also reports that 54% of pharma respondents expect at least some increase in insourcing, which raises the bar for CDMOs to prove what they bring.

seccions.titol: One page per modality, with scale and phase
seccions.text:
The most useful part of the site is a page for each modality you run. Monoclonal antibodies, viral vectors, cell therapy and microbial proteins have different buyers and different questions. Each page should answer the same set of points, so a sponsor can compare you with other providers in a few minutes.
For cell and gene therapy, also say which GMP framework you work under. The European Commission publishes dedicated GMP guidelines for advanced therapy medicinal products in Part IV of EudraLex Volume 4, in operation since 22 May 2018.

seccions.titol: How to state GMP status and inspection history without empty claims
seccions.text:
Writing GMP facility on a page does little for the person who has to sign the contract. The sponsor wants to know which authority inspected each site, for which activities and when. The European Medicines Agency explains that after inspecting a site, EU authorities issue either a GMP certificate or a non-compliance statement, and both are entered in EudraGMDP, a publicly accessible database.
Since the sponsor can check, it is better to say it yourself, precisely. Give the site, the authority, the scope and the year of the last inspection, plus any inspections by other agencies such as the FDA. If a site is not certified yet, say what stage it is at. An inflated claim costs more trust than a modest fact.

seccions.titol: Tech transfer steps and capacity windows
seccions.text:
The sponsor's next question is how much time and effort it will take to move the process to your site. Describe the tech transfer stages as you actually run them, who leads the project and which documents you need from the client. A simple diagram or a short animation explains this better than a long block of text.
Capacity sells too. If you can publish when suites or bioreactors have open slots, do it and keep it current. If you cannot make it public, add a form that asks for phase, scale and target date, so business development can reply with a concrete slot rather than a vague promise.

seccions.titol: How to show proof when everything is under NDA
seccions.text:
Most CDMO projects sit under confidentiality agreements, but that does not mean you have nothing to show. You can describe anonymised cases with the modality, scale, problem and what was done, always with the client's permission. Conference posters and talks also work, as do real profiles of your scientific leads.
Think about who is reading, too. The CSO wants data and named people. QA wants to see the quality system and the inspection record. Procurement wants to understand how quotes and planning work. A site that only speaks to one of them leaves the others without answers, and the project stalls.

seccions.titol: A contact form built for an RFP
seccions.text:
The journey should end in a form that asks for what business development needs to reply well. Ask for too much and sponsors abandon it. Ask for too little and the first call is wasted collecting basic details you could already have had.
Add a downloadable capabilities deck and, if you sell outside Spain, make sure the site works fully in English. It also helps when every modality page has its own title and description, so it shows up when someone searches for, say, a viral vector CDMO in Europe.

faqs.q: Should a CDMO publish prices on its website?
faqs.a: Usually not, because every project depends on modality, scale and phase. What helps is explaining how you build a quote, what information you need and when the team replies, provided it is a timeline you can keep. Sponsors then know what to expect and come to the first call with the right data ready.

faqs.q: Can we show our clients' logos?
faqs.a: Only with written permission. In this sector many confidentiality agreements forbid it, and a logo published without consent can do more harm than good. If you do not have permission, describe anonymised cases with modality, scale and technical outcome, and show the people who actually run the projects.

faqs.q: Does a CRO need the same kind of website as a CDMO?
faqs.a: The structure is the same but the content changes. A CRO should show the types of studies it runs, therapeutic areas, the team and the quality standards it works to, such as good laboratory or clinical practice. The goal does not change, which is letting the sponsor shortlist you before getting in touch.

faqs.q: Are Google Ads worth it for a CDMO?
faqs.a: They can be for very specific searches, such as a modality in a region, but only if the landing page answers what the sponsor is looking for. Before paying for clicks, make sure the modality pages exist and the form captures the right details. Otherwise the ads bring visits that never turn into requests.

bio-web-distribuidor-laboratori.intro: A lab equipment distributor's website has to explain what the manufacturer cannot. Which brands and models you carry locally, what stock and field service are nearby, who handles installation and qualification, and who the customer calls when the instrument stops. If the site just copies the manufacturer's product pages, it competes with the manufacturer's own website and loses.

seccions.titol: What buyers look for on a distributor's website
seccions.text:
Someone landing on a distributor's site usually knows which instrument they want, or at least what type. It could be a university lab manager, a hospital purchasing officer or a process engineer at a pharma company. They have read the specifications on the manufacturer's website. They come to yours to confirm that you can sell it to them, when it will arrive and who will support them afterwards.
That is why the questions your site must answer are very local.
