That is good news for anyone building bioreactors, TFF systems or process skids. These are project purchases that usually go through a URS and several rounds of quotes.
If projects are coming back, buyers need to find you while they are still writing the URS. That calls for product pages with useful data, scale-up stories from lab to production, 3D renders that show the equipment in a cleanroom and an obvious way to request a quote or a demo.

seccions.titol: Asia/Pacific is the fastest-growing region
seccions.text:
Asia/Pacific grew 10.6% in constant currencies to €524 million, and Sartorius notes that China contributed positively. EMEA, the largest market at €982 million, rose 6.5%. The Americas grew 7.6% excluding tariff compensation and 3.9% including it.
Every region contributed. For a mid-sized supplier, the sensible reading is to keep Europe as the base and check whether your website, distributor network and English-language material are ready for Asian enquiries that come in through search, trade shows or global accounts.

seccions.titol: US tariffs and how to communicate pricing and terms
seccions.text:
Sartorius Stedim Biotech received refunds of tariffs struck down by the US Supreme Court and is compensating customers for the surcharges they had paid. That lowers reported sales, but the company says the net effect on profitability is neutral. It also notes that changes in trade policy now play a bigger role.
If you sell into the United States, spell out in every quote who pays the duties, which Incoterm applies, how long the price is valid and what happens if the rules change. A terms page or a short FAQ written for procurement teams prevents misunderstandings.

seccions.titol: Process intensification and advanced therapies as product messages
seccions.text:
The new products Sartorius Stedim Biotech highlights are framed around what the customer gains. A single-use bioreactor bag with an improved sparger for better oxygen transfer is presented as a way to intensify upstream processing and get higher output from smaller bioreactor volumes.
For advanced therapies, the release mentions ready-to-use cytokines in closed sterile bags and a new animal-component-free cell culture medium. In your own marketing, lead with the outcome for the customer, such as more product from less volume or fewer open steps, and back it up with the spec sheet.

seccions.titol: How Danaher, Merck and Thermo Fisher compare in the third quarter
seccions.text:
Sartorius is not alone. The other big bioprocess suppliers that reported in October and November 2026 also describe steady demand, led by consumables and by the units that sell into drug manufacturing.
Each company reports in its own way, with different periods and segments, so the figures are not directly comparable. What they share is the direction. For a mid-sized supplier, it is a sign that the market is recovering across the board, not just for one brand.

faqs.q: What do Sartorius 2026 results say about the bioprocessing market?
faqs.a: That demand is growing in every region. In the first nine months, Sartorius Stedim Biotech sold €2,289 million, up 6.5% in constant currencies, or 7.8% excluding tariff compensation. Consumables remain the main driver, and the bioprocess equipment business grew compared with the same period last year.

faqs.q: Which region is growing fastest in bioprocessing according to Sartorius?
faqs.a: Asia/Pacific, up 10.6% in constant currencies to €524 million over nine months, with a positive contribution from China. EMEA remains the largest market at €982 million, up 6.5%. The Americas grew 7.6% excluding tariff compensation and 3.9% including it, because the compensation paid to customers is deducted from sales.

faqs.q: How should an equipment supplier explain tariffs to customers?
faqs.a: Clearly and in writing. Every quote should state who pays the duties, which Incoterm applies, how long the price holds and what happens if the rules change. Sartorius compensates its customers for surcharges they paid, but each company handles this its own way. What matters is that the buyer understands it before signing the order.

web-lenta-core-web-vitals.intro: To find out whether your website is slow, check the real-user data in PageSpeed Insights or the Core Web Vitals report in Search Console, and look at mobile first. Google treats a page as good when its main content appears within 2.5 seconds, it responds to taps within 200 milliseconds and the layout barely shifts while loading. The 0 to 100 score helps you find the cause, but it is not the number that counts.

seccions.titol: What Google measures when it calls a site slow
seccions.text:
Google measures speed with three metrics it calls Core Web Vitals. LCP is how long the largest element on screen takes to appear, usually an image or a large block of text. INP measures how quickly the page reacts when someone taps a button or opens a menu. CLS measures how much the layout moves around while the page loads.
To pass, all three need to be in the green for at least 75% of visits. Google assesses mobile and desktop separately, so a site that loads quickly on your office computer can still fail on a phone.

seccions.titol: Where to check your website speed for free
seccions.text:
The quickest option is PageSpeed Insights, a free Google tool. Paste in the address of a page and you get two blocks. At the top is real-user data from Chrome visitors over the last 28 days. Below it is a lab test that loads the page in a simulated environment and suggests fixes.
If your site is set up in Search Console, the Core Web Vitals report shows the whole site at a glance. It groups similar pages, splits mobile from desktop and labels each group Good, Need improvement or Poor based on its worst metric. A group only appears once it has enough LCP and CLS data.

seccions.titol: Why the 0 to 100 performance score is not what matters
seccions.text:
The 0 to 100 score comes from the lab test, which is run by Lighthouse. Google calls 90 or above good and anything under 50 poor, but the test simulates a single device on a fixed connection. Use it to find what slows a page down. To see what your customers actually experience, look at the real-user data at the top.
If a page is new or gets few visits, Google does not have enough real-user data for it. PageSpeed Insights then falls back to data for the whole site, and if there is still not enough, it shows none. At that point the lab test is your only clue. Run it on two or three key pages, such as the home page, a product page and the contact page.

seccions.titol: What usually slows down a business website
seccions.text:
On a business website, the largest element visible when a page opens is usually the hero image or a block of text. If that image is too heavy or loads late, LCP goes up. So the first questions are which image appears first, how large the file is and whether the server responds quickly enough.
Layout shifts happen when something loads late and pushes down what was already on screen. According to web.dev, the usual causes are images or videos without set dimensions, web fonts that render at a different size and third-party ads or widgets that resize themselves.

seccions.titol: Does a faster website rank higher on Google?
seccions.text:
Google says Core Web Vitals are used by its ranking systems and recommends getting them right. It also says that good scores do not guarantee top positions, and that it always tries to show the most relevant content even when the page experience is poor.
When there is plenty of helpful content for the same search, a good page experience can help. For a small business, though, the main reason to fix a slow site is customers. If a product page is slow to load on a phone or the booking button does not respond, the visitor may leave before getting in touch.

seccions.titol: What to ask your web designer or developer
seccions.text:
When you commission a new site or an improvement, ask for speed to be measured with data rather than gut feeling. A handful of clear questions is enough, whether you put them to an agency or to the person who looks after your site.
After a change, real-user data takes time to move because it covers the last 28 days. The lab test updates straight away, so use it to confirm the fix works, except for INP, which it cannot measure because nobody taps the page. In Search Console, validating a fix starts a 28-day monitoring period.

faqs.q: Is PageSpeed Insights free?
faqs.a: Yes. PageSpeed Insights is a free Google tool that runs in your browser. Enter the page address, pick mobile or desktop and you get real-user data, if there is enough, plus a lab test with suggestions. The real-user data covers the last 28 days.

faqs.q: Why is my mobile score lower than my desktop score?
faqs.a: The mobile test simulates a mid-range phone on a mobile network, while the desktop test uses a wired connection. So it is normal for the mobile score to come out lower, and it does not mean your site is broken. Focus on the real-user data for mobile and treat the score as a pointer to what can be improved.

faqs.q: What does "No data available" mean in Search Console?
faqs.a: It means either your Search Console property is new or the Chrome User Experience Report does not yet have enough data on your site for that device type. If the property is new, the data can take a few days to appear. In the meantime, run the PageSpeed Insights lab test on your most important pages.

faqs.q: Do I need a new website if mine is slow?
faqs.a: Not always. Often it is enough to compress images, set their dimensions and remove or delay third-party tools you do not need. If the problem lies in the theme or the server and shows up on every page, it is worth comparing whether fixing the current site or rebuilding it makes more sense.

bio-estudi-mercat-dades-publiques.intro: A life science supplier can run its own market research on five free public databases. ClinicalTrials.gov and the EU clinical trials website show who is developing what, the EMA lists authorised medicines, CORDIS shows who is doing EU-funded research and Eurostat shows trade flows. For the study to support a decision and be cited by Google and AI answers, it has to state the source, download date, filters and method.

seccions.titol: Which market questions public registries can answer
seccions.text:
A public registry answers questions you can count. How many trials there are for a modality in a country, which companies hold biosimilar authorisations, which research groups work with bioreactors or which countries buy the most of a product. For a bioprocess equipment maker, a consumables supplier, a CDMO or a distributor, those answers show where the activity is and who is worth talking to.
No registry will tell you why a customer would buy or what they think of your competitors. That takes interviews, distributors and a close look at the competition, which we cover in the guide to market analysis for new equipment.

seccions.titol: Five free databases and the question each one answers
seccions.text: The five databases that help a supplier in this sector most are free and can be downloaded. Each one answers a different question and comes in its own format. The table sums up what you will find in each, so you can pick by the question you have.

seccions.titol: ClinicalTrials.gov and CTIS show who is developing what
seccions.text:
ClinicalTrials.gov has a public REST API, now at version 2, that returns the studies matching a query and a set of filters. You can search by condition, intervention, sponsor or location, filter by status and get the results as JSON or CSV. With the countTotal parameter, the API also returns the total number of studies for the query.
For Europe, the EU clinical trials website, which runs on the CTIS system, holds information on trials in the EU and the European Economic Area since 31 January 2022. Trials started before then are in the EU Clinical Trials Register. You can download search results as CSV and follow a search by RSS.
One worked example is our count of monoclonal antibody trials in Europe, based on a dated ClinicalTrials.gov download with stated filters. A late-stage trial is not a purchase order, but it can mean the sponsor is already thinking about scale-up and manufacturing capacity.

seccions.titol: EMA, CORDIS and Eurostat for medicines, research and trade
seccions.text:
The EMA publishes downloadable tables of centrally authorised medicines, orphan designations and medicine shortages, among others. The website refreshes them overnight and also offers its content in JSON. With the medicines table you can count biosimilars by molecule, by marketing authorisation holder and by year.
CORDIS releases Horizon Europe project data every month, with participating organisations, topics, deliverables, publications and report summaries. It warns that the files may not fully match the live website. It is the basis of our count of bioprocess projects in Horizon Europe by country and type of organisation.
Eurostat's Comext database covers trade in goods for the EU, its member states and many non-EU countries, with monthly and annual CSV files going back to January 1988. For a distributor or an exporter, it shows which countries buy the most of a product family.

seccions.titol: How to make your count reproducible
seccions.text:
A count is only worth something if someone else can repeat it and get the same number. So write everything down while you work, not at the end. When someone in sales or management asks where a figure comes from, the answer should be a specific query run on a specific date.
The method paragraph should also state the limits. A trial that does not use your search term will not show up, one project can count in several countries and the current year is incomplete. Stating the limits makes readers trust the figure and stops anyone using it for something it does not show.

seccions.titol: Publish the study so Google and AI answers can cite it
seccions.text:
A study of your own, published on your website, does two jobs. Internally, it helps you choose markets, accounts and messages. Externally, it is original content with a specific figure, a method and downloadable data, the kind of page that search engines and AI answers can cite as a source. That is why it is part of our SEO work.
The page should give the main figure in its first sentence, with its base, and explain how it was counted in a section of its own. Add a chart with the same figures, the download date and a CSV. If you repeat it every year with the same method, you can compare years and the page stays current.
At crida studio we run these studies as part of our marketing for biotech, bioprocess and pharma companies. We choose the question with the sales team, download and count the data, write up the method and publish the page in Catalan, Spanish and English. We do not promise rankings or citations, because they depend on Google, AI tools and the competition.

faqs.q: Do I need to code to do market research with public data?
faqs.a: Not always. The EMA publishes its tables in Excel and CORDIS in CSV and XLSX, and both can be filtered in a spreadsheet. ClinicalTrials.gov also returns results as CSV. A short Python script helps when you want to repeat the count every month with the same filters.

faqs.q: Can I publish a count based on these registries on my website?
faqs.a: It depends on each registry's terms. CORDIS, for example, publishes its data under the European Commission reuse notice. For the others, read the terms of use before you publish. In every case, cite the source and the download date and link to the original registry so anyone can check the figures.

faqs.q: How often should the study be updated?
faqs.a: It depends on the registry and on the decision it supports. The EMA refreshes its tables overnight and CORDIS releases files monthly, but a market study does not need to keep that pace. For most suppliers, repeating it once a year or before a major trade show is enough, as long as the method stays the same.

bio-medicaments-ema-2025-proveidors.intro: In 2025, the EMA's human medicines committee, the CHMP, adopted 104 positive opinions, 38 of them for a new active substance. There were 41 biosimilars, the highest number ever, 23 of them containing denosumab, and only 4 advanced therapies. If you sell equipment, consumables or manufacturing capacity, this mix tells you which buyers to put first, what to say to them and when.

seccions.titol: What the EMA recommended in 2025
seccions.text:
The EMA recommended 104 human medicines in 2025 and adopted a negative opinion on 7. Companies withdrew 22 applications before the assessment was finished. Of the 104, 38 had an active substance never authorised in the EU before. The EMA released these figures with its annual report on 11 June 2026, and the detail is in its Human medicines in 2025 overview.
These are recommendations, not authorisations. The EMA sends each opinion to the European Commission, which adopts the EU-wide marketing authorisation. The authorisation comes after the opinion, so an opinion adopted late in the year can become an authorisation the following year. That is why counts by authorisation date give different figures.

seccions.titol: A record year for biosimilars, led by denosumab
seccions.text:
Biosimilars were the largest group in 2025. The CHMP gave a positive opinion to 41, its highest number ever, and 23 of them contain denosumab, a monoclonal antibody for osteoporosis and bone loss. Since the biosimilar framework was set up in 2005, the committee has assessed 181 applications and approved 165.
The EMA presents biosimilars as a core tool for managing costs and widening access. Our guide to biosimilars authorised by the EMA counts 44 for 2025, 26 of them denosumab, because it counts products still authorised on 3 November 2026 by their Commission authorisation date. This report counts the committee's opinions in 2025. Both figures are right and measure different steps.

seccions.titol: Few advanced therapies, all with a new active substance
seccions.text:
Only 4 of the 104 recommendations were advanced therapy medicinal products, or ATMPs. They are Aucatzyl, a CAR-T therapy for a type of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, Zemcelpro, an umbilical cord stem cell therapy for blood cancers, and Vyjuvek and Waskyra, two gene therapies for rare diseases. All four have a new active substance and three came through the PRIME scheme.
The 7 negative opinions include Elevidys, for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, and Jelrix, made from the patient's own cartilage-forming cells for knee cartilage defects. In therapies such as Aucatzyl or Waskyra, each dose is made from the patient's own cells, so batches are small and each one has to be tracked. Our count of cell and gene therapy trials in Spain helps show who works in this field.

seccions.titol: Which buyers to target
seccions.text: The 2025 mix points to three buyer groups with different needs. Before you split the budget, check how much weight each group carries in your customer base and where you have the strongest references to show.

seccions.titol: What messages and web content to prepare
seccions.text:
Each group needs its own page on your site, with its problem in the headline. A biosimilars page can show how to move from lab to production on the same platform. An advanced therapies page can show the closed system and the paperwork. Both need datasheets and case studies people can download.
The EMA figures also work as material for your own content, such as an article or a customer email. Always cite the source and make clear these are recommendations. Putting this order in place is part of a supplier's marketing strategy, and it is worth doing before the trade show season.

seccions.titol: Trade show conversations and buying timelines
seccions.text:
On the stand, the 2025 report gives you an easy opening question. Ask each visitor whether they work on a biosimilar, a new active substance or an advanced therapy, and tailor the demo to the answer. If you are getting ready for a show like ACHEMA or CPHI, bring separate material for each group.
Timing matters too. Accelerated assessment, which 3 medicines received in 2025, takes 150 days at most instead of 210. We have no data on when each company buys. Our reading is that much of the process buying happens before the application, while manufacturing is being set up. If you wait for the recommendation news, you may be too late.

seccions.titol: How to read the figures in the report
seccions.text:
The categories overlap. One medicine can be a new active substance, an orphan, a PRIME medicine and an advanced therapy at once, as Zemcelpro is. The 16 orphans are those whose designation was confirmed by the end of 2025. And the 41 biosimilars include three duplicates, the same medicine under another brand name.
The report does not say how much will sell or who makes each medicine. To turn the figures into an account list, cross them with the holder of each authorisation and with ongoing trials. That is the work we do at crida studio in marketing for biotech and bioprocess companies, without promising results that depend on each market.

faqs.q: How many medicines did the EMA recommend in 2025?
faqs.a: The EMA adopted 104 positive opinions on human medicines in 2025 and 7 negative ones, while companies withdrew 22 applications. Of the 104, 38 had a new active substance in the EU, 41 were biosimilars and 10 were generics. These are recommendations the EMA sends to the European Commission, which adopts the authorisation.

faqs.q: How many denosumab biosimilars did the EMA recommend in 2025?
faqs.a: 23 of the 41 biosimilars with a positive opinion in 2025 contain denosumab, a monoclonal antibody for osteoporosis, bone loss and other bone problems. According to the EMA, 41 is the highest number of biosimilars it has ever approved in a year. For a supplier, it means many products competing on the same molecule.

faqs.q: Which advanced therapies did the EMA recommend in 2025?
faqs.a: Four. Aucatzyl, a CAR-T therapy for leukaemia, Zemcelpro, an umbilical cord cell therapy for blood cancers, and Vyjuvek and Waskyra, two gene therapies for rare diseases of the skin and the blood. All four have a new active substance and three came through the PRIME scheme.

search-console-que-mirar-cada-mes.intro: Google suggests checking Search Console roughly once a month, and it emails you when it finds a new issue. A monthly visit needs four checks. Compare clicks and impressions with the previous month, separate searches for your name from those that bring new customers, confirm your key pages are indexed and note what you changed on the site.

seccions.titol: How often should you check Search Console?
seccions.text:
Once a month is enough for most business websites. Google's getting started guide says you don't need to log in every day, because it emails you when it detects issues. It suggests checking your account about once a month, or whenever you change the content of your site.
For that visit to be useful, the property must be verified and the sitemap submitted. Google says it can find your pages without a sitemap, but submitting one may speed things up and lets you see its data. Do it once, then check that the Sitemaps report shows no errors.

seccions.titol: How to read the Performance report without getting lost
seccions.text:
The Performance report shows how often your site appeared on Google and how many people clicked through. An impression means your site was shown in the results and a click is a visit. CTR is clicks divided by impressions. Average position is worked out from your site's topmost result in each search.
By default the report covers the last three months. Switch the chart to the monthly view and daily ups and downs, such as weekends or holidays, matter less, so the trend is easier to read. Then open the Pages tab and see which pages gained or lost clicks compared with the previous month.
This check won't tell you whether your site shows up in Google's AI Mode, which you measure in a different way. Here the focus is on regular searches that send visitors to your service pages.

seccions.titol: Separate branded searches from those that bring new customers
seccions.text:
The most telling figure is how many clicks come from people who didn't know you yet. Someone who types the name of your clinic was already looking for you. Someone who types dentist in Girona has just found you. If only branded searches grow, the site serves existing customers but doesn't bring in new ones.
On 20 November 2025, Google announced a branded and non-branded queries filter for the Performance report, and since 11 March 2026 it has been available to all eligible sites. Google says an internal AI-assisted system sorts the queries and also catches typos in your name. A new card in the Insights report shows how clicks are split.
It only appears for top-level properties and for sites with enough queries and impressions. If your site is small and you don't have it, filter the queries that contain your company name by hand and compare them with the rest.

seccions.titol: Are your key pages indexed?
seccions.text:
Make sure the pages that bring you customers appear on Google. Google's help page says that if your site has fewer than 500 pages, you probably don't need the Page indexing report. Search Google for your key pages and, if they don't show up, open the report to find out why.
Some unindexed pages are normal. Google explains that duplicates shouldn't be indexed, and neither should pages with a noindex tag or deleted pages that return a 404 error. What matters is that your home page and service pages are in. If you fix an issue and click Validate fix, Google says validation typically takes up to about two weeks, and sometimes much longer.
If many of your service pages are missing, it's worth checking whether your business can be found and understood before you publish anything else. A new blog post won't help much while the pages that explain what you do are still missing from Google.

seccions.titol: Note on the chart what you changed on the site
seccions.text:
Three months later, nobody remembers why a chart dropped. On 17 November 2025, Google added custom annotations to the Performance charts in Search Console. Right-click the chart, choose Add annotation, pick the date and write a note of up to 120 characters.
Google suggests noting template changes, migrations, new plugins, hiring an agency or outside events such as holidays. For a business on the Costa Brava, the start and end of the season are worth noting too. Everyone with access to the property can see the notes, so leave out sensitive personal data.

seccions.titol: The monthly check in one table
seccions.text: The table sums up what to look at in each report and which signal means you should act. If the same alerts keep coming back or non-branded searches don't grow, it's time to bring in an SEO service that looks at content and technical issues together.

faqs.q: Do I need to check Search Console every day?
faqs.a: No. Google says there's no need to log in daily, because it emails you when it finds new issues on your site. It suggests checking about once a month, or whenever you change your content. If you're migrating or redesigning the site, it's worth looking more often that month.

faqs.q: Why can't I see the branded queries filter?
faqs.a: Google only offers it for top-level properties, not for a folder or subdomain property, and only for sites with enough queries and impressions. A small site may not get it. In the meantime, filter the queries that contain your company name to separate them yourself.

faqs.q: Is it bad to have pages that aren't indexed?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Google says you shouldn't expect every URL on your site to be indexed. Duplicates, pages with a noindex tag and deleted pages should stay out. What you should watch is that your home page and service pages are indexed.

faqs.q: Who can see the annotations I add to the chart?
faqs.a: Everyone with access to the Search Console property can see them, such as your agency or whoever manages the site. That's why Google advises against adding sensitive personal information. Each note can be up to 120 characters long and is tied to a specific date.

bio-biblioteca-notes-aplicacio.intro: An application notes library works when every note has its own HTML page, with the summary, key data, author and date as text, and the full PDF alongside. The PDF sends a canonical header pointing to that page, any form gates only the complete document, and the library can be filtered by application, scale and technique.

seccions.titol: Why every application note needs its own HTML page
seccions.text:
Google can index a PDF. Adobe PDF is on its list of indexable file types, next to HTML, Word and Excel. The trouble starts once someone lands on it from search. They open the PDF on its own, outside the site, with no path to the product page or to a contact form.
One page per note fixes that. It carries a title with the application and scale, a three or four line summary, the key data as text or in a table, and the PDF to download. Readers see at once whether the note is relevant, and the summary and data sit on the page as text rather than inside a file.

seccions.titol: How to stop the PDF competing with its own page
seccions.text:
If the page and the PDF say the same thing, you have two URLs with very similar content. Google explains that the HTML canonical element only works on HTML pages, and that for files such as PDFs you can send a rel canonical HTTP header instead. The same logic applies to an equipment datasheet.
Whoever runs the server sets the header, and it must point to the full URL of the note's page, including https. Google treats it as a strong signal and says these methods stack. So the sitemap should list the note's page rather than the PDF, and every internal link should go to the page.

seccions.titol: Where the form goes on each note's page
seccions.text: Which notes are worth gating and which to leave open is covered in our guide on white paper, application note or webinar. For the library, what matters is where the form sits. The summary and key data stay open on the note's page, and the form, if there is one, asks for a few details in exchange for the full PDF. That way the part that answers the search is visible to everyone, Google included.

seccions.titol: What Google should see when the full note needs registration
seccions.text:
If you want Google to index a note that readers only see after registering, Google has structured data for subscription and paywalled content that also covers registration. You mark the page with isAccessibleForFree set to false and use hasPart with a CSS class selector to show which part is gated. If you do not want the gated document indexed, Google says none of this is needed.
That markup helps Google tell gated content apart from cloaking, which breaks its spam policies. Cloaking means showing search engines one thing and people another in order to manipulate rankings. Google says a paywall or content gate is not cloaking as long as Google can see the full content, just like anyone with access, and you follow its Flexible Sampling guidance.

seccions.titol: Filters for application, scale and technique, and links from every product page
seccions.text:
People looking for an application note think about their own process. So the library should filter by application, such as monoclonal antibodies, vaccines or cell therapy, by scale, from lab to production, and by technique, such as bioreactor culture or tangential flow filtration.
Each product page should link to the notes run on that equipment, and each note should link back to the product page of the equipment used. That way an engineer who arrives through a note reaches the product, and one who arrives through the product finds the evidence. Third-party papers that cite the equipment belong on a separate page, because you did not write them.

seccions.titol: Author, date and version on every note
seccions.text:
Each note should say who produced it, usually the application scientist or engineer who ran the test, and when it was published. Google recommends a visible, prominent date labelled with words such as Published or Last updated, and the same date in structured data through datePublished and dateModified.
The visible date and the structured data date must match. Google also asks you not to use future dates and to give the date of the page, not of the experiment it describes. If a note changes because of new equipment or new data, show the version on the PDF and the update date on the page.

faqs.q: Does Google index application notes in PDF?
faqs.a: Yes. PDF is on the list of file types Google can index. But a standalone PDF does not take readers to the product page or to a contact form, and it rarely says who wrote it or when. That is why each note is better off with its own HTML page, with the summary and key data, and a canonical header on the PDF pointing to that page.

faqs.q: If I add a form, does Google stop seeing the note?
faqs.a: It depends on what you want indexed. If the full registration-only document should appear in Google, Google needs to see all of it, just like a registered reader, and the page needs the structured data for subscription content. If you do not want it indexed, Google says no markup is needed, and the open page with the summary stays visible to everyone.

faqs.q: Should old application notes be taken down?
faqs.a: Not if the data is still correct for equipment you sell. If the equipment is discontinued, say so on the page and link to the model that replaces it. If a note genuinely changes, update its version and date. Changing only the date to make it look fresh gives readers nothing and costs you their trust.

bio-sector-biotec-espanya-asebio-2025.intro: The 2025 AseBio Report, presented in Madrid in June 2026, counts 1,119 biotech companies in Spain in 2025, up 10.4% on the previous year. Of these, 52% are micro firms and 43.6% are SMEs, almost one in four is in Catalonia, and capital raised rose from 181 to 408 million euros. For a supplier, that means segmenting by region and field and selling to small companies.

seccions.titol: How many biotech companies are there in Spain in 2025
seccions.text:
According to the 2025 AseBio Report, Spain has 1,119 biotech companies in 2025, up 10.4% on the previous year. Their activity generated 13.271 billion euros in income in 2024, 1.2% of Spanish GDP, and supported 158,366 jobs.
Company size is the figure that changes marketing most. Microenterprises make up 52% of these companies and SMEs 43.6%. In firms this small there is often no purchasing department or in-house engineering team. Your website and catalogues need to explain the equipment, installation and service to someone who may be deciding alone.
AseBio presented the 2025 AseBio Report, which focuses on the Biotech Act, in Madrid in June 2026. The full report is a PDF you can download from the AseBio website after filling in a short form with your details. Below are the key figures AseBio released, each with the year it refers to.

seccions.titol: Where Spanish biotech companies are, region by region
seccions.text:
Catalonia ranks first, with 23.32% of biotech companies. Next come Madrid with 18.68%, Andalusia with 12.33%, the Basque Country with 9.65% and the Valencian Community with 8.85%. Together these five regions hold more than seven in ten companies in the sector.
For a supplier based in Catalonia, the home market is almost one in four Spanish biotechs, and the other three are elsewhere. That calls for Spanish-language content, Google Ads campaigns with regional targeting and a visit plan covering Madrid, Andalusia, the Basque Country and Valencia. For Catalonia itself, the BioRegion of Catalonia report goes into more detail.

seccions.titol: Human health leads and food biotech is growing
seccions.text:
Human health is still the main field, with 55.5% of companies, down from 58% the previous year. Food comes second with 32.6%, up from 27% in 2023. Then come animal health and aquaculture, agriculture and forestry, the environment and industrial biotechnology.
If your website only talks about pharma, you miss a growing part of the market. A food company that runs fermentation or develops ingredients searches with different words and wants different examples. Build pages and case studies for each field you serve, in its own vocabulary, instead of one page for everyone.

seccions.titol: Record investment in 2025 and what it means for sales
seccions.text:
Capital raised went from 181 million euros in 2024 to 408 million in 2025, a 125% increase. Deals rose from 52 to 59, with an average size of nearly 7 million euros. Capital increases involving international investors brought in 302 million across 12 transactions.
Biotech companies invested 1.46 billion euros in R&D in 2024, up 13.9%. Companies fund 67% of it from their own resources, and AseBio notes a significant rise in spending on physical infrastructure. For equipment suppliers, a closed round is a good moment to get back in touch, and a useful signal when you score startup leads in your CRM.

seccions.titol: Partnerships with research centres mean two buyers
seccions.text:
Spanish biotechs set up 266 partnerships in 2025. Of these, 168 were with research centres or foundations, 50 with other biotech companies and 40 with other types of companies. Working with research is by far the most common kind of partnership in the sector.
In practice, one project can have two buyers. The company pays or leads, while the research group uses the equipment and has its say. Prepare content for both, with datasheets and references for the group and cost and service arguments for the company. Trade shows such as BioSpain or Farmaforum are places where you can meet both.

seccions.titol: What to change in your marketing plan
seccions.text:
With these figures, a supplier can review its plan on five points. Most of them come down to putting each euro and each message in a better place. These are the points we look at when we build a marketing strategy for a supplier in the sector.
If you sell bioprocess equipment, consumables or services in Spain, biotech marketing has to start from this picture of the market. A generic list of pharma companies leaves out most biotechs, which are small and spread across the whole country.

seccions.titol: How to read the AseBio figures
seccions.text:
The AseBio release mixes years. Company numbers, capital raised and partnerships are for 2025. Income, share of GDP and R&D spending are for 2024. The food figure is compared with 2023. When you quote a figure in a presentation or on your website, always give the year.
The fields add up to more than 100% because one company can work in several. Biocat's report on Catalonia, by contrast, counts the 1,650 companies in the whole life sciences and health sector, with subsectors such as medtech and digital health. It uses a different scope, so its figures cannot be added to AseBio's or compared with them directly.

faqs.q: How many biotech companies are there in Spain?
faqs.a: According to the 2025 AseBio Report, there are 1,119 in 2025, up 10.4% on the previous year. Microenterprises make up 52% and SMEs 43.6%. Human health is the main field, with 55.5% of companies, and food is second with 32.6%.

faqs.q: Which Spanish region has the most biotech companies?
faqs.a: Catalonia, with 23.32% of Spain's biotech companies. It is followed by Madrid with 18.68%, Andalusia with 12.33%, the Basque Country with 9.65% and the Valencian Community with 8.85%. For a supplier, the market goes well beyond Catalonia and Madrid, so plan for all five regions.

faqs.q: How much investment did Spanish biotechs raise in 2025?
faqs.a: According to AseBio, 408 million euros across 59 deals, compared with 181 million in 2024. That is a record and a 125% increase. International investors played a key role, with 302 million in 12 capital increases, and CDTI Innvierte put 47.2 million into rounds at 10 companies.

bio-terapies-avancades-autoritzades-ema.intro: We counted 24 advanced therapies authorised in the EU in the EMA's public medicines file, downloaded on 22 November 2026. Since 2009, 33 have been authorised, and 9 of them no longer are. On the EMA committee's list, 22 of 31 are gene therapies. If you sell equipment, consumables or manufacturing services, this is a short list of named prospects.

seccions.titol: How many advanced therapies are authorised in the EU
seccions.text:
The EMA medicines file lists 24 advanced therapies for human use with the status authorised. According to the EMA, all advanced therapy medicines are authorised centrally through the agency, so this file covers every EU authorisation.
The EMA defines them as medicines for human use based on genes, tissues or cells. There are three main types, gene therapies, somatic cell therapies and tissue-engineered products. Since 2009, 33 have held an EU authorisation at some point, and 9 of them no longer do.

seccions.titol: How many have been approved since 2009
seccions.text:
Approvals have picked up, but the numbers are still small. Between 2009 and 2014 there were 4, and between 2015 and 2017 there were 5. Since 2018 each three-year period has brought 8, and the latest one is not over yet. 2026 already has 3, Waskyra in January, Adstiladrin in May and Itvisma in June. Waskyra is one of the advanced therapies the EMA recommended in 2025.
This count includes all 33 that have held an authorisation at some point, including those that later lost it. According to the EMA's Committee for Advanced Therapies, 50 applications were submitted between 2009 and February 2026, with 32 positive opinions, 7 negative ones and 13 withdrawals. Cell and gene therapy clinical trials show what may come next.

seccions.titol: Most approved ATMPs are gene therapies
seccions.text:
The Committee for Advanced Therapies list from March 2026 has 31 products. 22 are gene therapies, 5 are somatic cell therapies and 4 are tissue-engineered products. The list includes withdrawn products and ends with Waskyra, authorised in January 2026.
CAR-T therapies such as Kymriah, Yescarta and Carvykti appear on that list as gene therapies. Cell and tissue products are fewer, and their holders include companies such as Holostem, CO.DON and Cordex Biologics. For a supplier, the therapy type tells you what kind of process sits behind each account.

seccions.titol: 9 of the 33 are no longer authorised
seccions.text:
Of the 33 advanced therapies that have been authorised, 9 no longer are. 7 are listed as withdrawn and 2 as expired. The withdrawn products include Zynteglo, authorised in 2019 and withdrawn in March 2022, and Beqvez, authorised in July 2024 and withdrawn in May 2025.
The file does not say why each one was withdrawn, and we do not guess here. What it does show is that an authorisation does not guarantee a product stays on the market. Skysona was authorised in July 2021 and, according to the committee's list, withdrawn in November of the same year.
For marketing, this means checking each account's status before running a campaign. A holder that has withdrawn a product may still have other projects under way, but the message and the timing will be different.

seccions.titol: Who holds the approved advanced therapies
seccions.text:
The 24 authorised products belong to 18 holders. Novartis has 4, Kymriah, Zolgensma, Luxturna and Itvisma. Fondazione Telethon, Bristol-Myers Squibb and Kite Pharma have 2 each. The rest have 1, from Ferring and Amgen to Autolus and Holostem. Next to EMA-approved biosimilars, which are far more numerous, this is a market with very few names.
The flags in the file add context. 17 of the 24 are orphan medicines, 14 went through the EMA's PRIME scheme and 8 have a conditional marketing authorisation. 22 are under additional monitoring, and 9 carry ATC code L01, the code for antineoplastic agents.

seccions.titol: How to use this list in your marketing
seccions.text:
With 24 products and 18 holders, this market calls for an account-by-account marketing strategy. The whole list fits in a spreadsheet, and each name comes with a therapy, a date and a status that are all public. The holder is not always the manufacturer, but it is the first name to check.
Our marketing for biotech companies service turns public data like this into target account lists, a message for each type of buyer and the web pages those buyers will check, without promising results that depend on each market.

seccions.titol: How we counted and what the data does not say
seccions.text:
We downloaded the Medicines output, medicines report file from the EMA's Download medicine data page. The EMA generated it on 22 November 2026 at 18.00 and we downloaded it the same day. We took the rows with category Human and the Advanced therapy flag set to Yes. That gives 36.
The flag is incomplete. Itvisma, authorised on 30 June 2026, has the same active substance as Zolgensma but is not flagged, and neither is an earlier withdrawn application for Roctavian. We added records with the same active substance as a flagged one, which gives 38, including the 33 authorised. All 31 products on the committee's list are there. For years we use the authorisation date.
There are limits. We count authorisations, not sales or patients treated. Some withdrawn or refused advanced therapy applications have no flag, such as Lumevoq, Artobend and Heparesc, so we do not give a total for applications. The therapy types come from the committee's March 2026 list, which does not include Adstiladrin or Itvisma. We have kept the list of the 38 records with names, statuses and dates.

faqs.q: How many cell and gene therapies are approved in Europe?
faqs.a: The EMA file downloaded on 22 November 2026 lists 24 advanced therapies authorised in the EU, from 18 holders. Since 2009, 33 have been authorised, and 9 of them no longer are. On the March 2026 list from the Committee for Advanced Therapies, 22 of the 31 products are gene therapies.

faqs.q: Where can I find the official EMA list of approved ATMPs?
faqs.a: There are two routes. The Medicines output file on the EMA's Download medicine data page can be filtered by the Advanced therapy column, although that flag is incomplete. The Committee for Advanced Therapies also publishes a quarterly report with the list of authorised products, their type and those withdrawn.

faqs.q: Why have some advanced therapies been withdrawn?
faqs.a: The EMA file only gives the status and the date, not the reason. Each row links to the medicine's page on the EMA website, which is where to look case by case. We do not interpret it here. What the file does show is that 9 of the 33 approved therapies are no longer authorised.

logo-favicon-google.intro: If your favicon isn't showing in Google and you see a globe instead, it's usually because Google can't find the icon on your home page, can't crawl it, or the icon doesn't meet its guidelines. If your old logo still appears, Google hasn't recrawled the home page yet or your site still declares the old icon. The fix is a small, square version of your logo, declared on the home page and crawlable by Google.

seccions.titol: What the globe next to your site name means
seccions.text:
The globe is Google's generic icon, shown when it isn't using one from your site. The small icon next to your site name in the results is your favicon. Google can show it when your site has one that meets its guidelines, but it warns that a favicon isn't guaranteed.
The name beside it is the site name. Google generates it automatically from your home page and from references to your site across the web. To suggest the name you prefer, Google says to add WebSite structured data to the home page.

seccions.titol: Where Google looks for your favicon
seccions.text:
Google only looks for the icon on your home page. The page needs a link tag in its header, with icon as the rel value, pointing to the file. Google also accepts shortcut icon and apple-touch-icon, the icon designed for iOS. The file can live on your own site or on another server, such as a CDN.
Google supports one favicon per hostname. A subdomain like shop.example.com can have its own icon. A subdirectory like example.com/shop can't, so it uses the home page icon. If your online shop or blog runs on a subdomain, check it separately.
Googlebot has to be able to crawl the home page and follow any redirects to the page where the icon is declared, and Googlebot-Image has to be able to crawl the icon file. If robots.txt or any other rule blocks them, Google won't show the icon. If the whole home page is blocked, it's worth checking whether your business can be found and understood.

seccions.titol: What size and format Google needs for a favicon
seccions.text:
The icon must be square and at least 8 by 8 pixels. Google recommends going larger than 48 by 48 pixels so it looks good on different surfaces. Supported formats are BMP, GIF, ICO, PNG, JPEG, PPM and TIFF.
SVG and WebP are not on the list. If your site only declares its icon in one of those formats, add a PNG or ICO version as well. If you've read that the icon has to be a multiple of 48 pixels, Google's current page doesn't ask for that.
Google also asks for an icon that represents your brand, so people can spot your site as they scan the results. A horizontal logo with the full name is hard to read in such a small square. A clinic or restaurant with a long name needs a reduced version of the logo, such as the symbol or the initial, that fits the brand system.

seccions.titol: Why Google still shows your old logo
seccions.text:
When you change the icon, Google has to recrawl the home page and process the new information. Google says crawling can take anywhere from several days to several weeks, depending on how often its systems decide the content needs refreshing. Imagine a Girona restaurant that has just rebranded. Until Google recrawls its home page, the old logo may keep showing in the results.
Before you wait, check that the home page already points to the new file, that no tag for the old one remains in the theme or a plugin, and that the icon URL doesn't change with every tweak, because Google asks for a stable one. Then you can request indexing of the home page with the URL Inspection tool in Google Search Console.

seccions.titol: Your favicon and your structured data logo are separate
seccions.text:
Organization structured data is another place where you can tell Google about your logo. It can help Google understand which logo you want it to show, for example in search results and knowledge panels. Google recommends adding it to your home page or to a single page about your organisation, such as the about page.
That logo has its own requirements. It must be at least 112 by 112 pixels, its URL must be crawlable and indexable, and the file format must be supported by Google Images. It also has to look right on a plain white background. So it makes sense to prepare the square icon and the full logo at the same time.

seccions.titol: What to prepare and what to ask your designer and web team
seccions.text:
Ask whoever designs your brand for the reduced version in a square, tested at small sizes, plus the full logo in high resolution. Ask whoever runs your website to go through each point on the list below and add Organization structured data.
If your site runs on WordPress, the site icon has been set under General Settings since version 6.5. The official documentation asks for a square image of at least 512 pixels on each side and recommends PNG. If you are commissioning a web design project, put the icon on the list of deliverables.

faqs.q: Why does Google show a globe instead of my logo?
faqs.a: It means Google isn't using any icon from your site. Your home page may not declare one, robots.txt may block the page or the file, or the image may not be square or in a supported format. Check those points and request indexing of the home page. Even then, Google says a favicon isn't guaranteed.

faqs.q: How long does Google take to show a new favicon?
faqs.a: Google says crawling can take anywhere from several days to several weeks. First check that the home page already points to the new file. Then you can request indexing of the home page with the URL Inspection tool in Search Console. Until Google recrawls it, the old icon may keep appearing in results.

faqs.q: Can my online shop have a different favicon from my main site?
faqs.a: It depends on where the shop lives. Google supports one favicon per hostname. If the shop is on a subdomain such as shop.example.com, it can have its own. If it sits in a folder such as example.com/shop, Google uses the home page icon. Check how your site is set up before designing two icons.

bio-critical-medicines-act-proveidors.intro: The EU Critical Medicines Act can open up business for bioprocess equipment and service suppliers, but only indirectly. It backs new or upgraded plants in the EU and public tenders that reward EU manufacturing, and what scores is where the medicine is made. As of November 2026 it is not law yet and article numbers may change, so talk about it with dates and without promises.

seccions.titol: Where the Critical Medicines Act stands in November 2026
seccions.text:
The European Commission proposed the regulation on 11 March 2025. The Council agreed its position on 2 December 2025 and the European Parliament adopted its own on 20 January 2026. The two reached a provisional agreement on 12 May 2026.
Coreper endorsed the agreed text on 30 June, and Parliament's public health committee approved it on 14 July. Parliament's Legislative Observatory gives 23 November 2026 as the indicative plenary date. Council adoption and publication in the Official Journal come after that. We quote article numbers from the Council's compromise text, and they may change in the final version.

seccions.titol: What it says about manufacturing capacity in the EU
seccions.text:
Strategic projects are the core of the act. Under Article 5, a project in the EU that creates, upgrades or expands manufacturing capacity qualifies if it meets at least one criterion. It can make critical medicines or their active substances, modernise an existing site, make key inputs, or help roll out in the EU a technology that is key to producing them.
Article 3 defines key inputs as materials other than the active substance that are needed to manufacture a medicine, including immediate packaging, excipients, solvents, reagents and starting materials. Its examples of innovative manufacturing processes include continuous manufacturing, decentralised manufacturing, platform technologies, AI and 3D technologies.
The benefits are faster paperwork and funding. The authority each country designates must decide within 20 days whether a project is strategic (Article 6). The national medicines authority must prioritise GMP inspections of the project's new, expanded or modernised sites (Article 11). Member states may prioritise financial support for projects that address an identified supply chain vulnerability (Article 15).

seccions.titol: Public procurement that looks beyond price
seccions.text:
Article 18 requires public buyers of critical medicines to apply resilience requirements, which must support more diverse sources of active substances and reward reliable suppliers. Buyers can apply them as selection criteria, technical specifications, best price-quality ratio or contract performance clauses.
Where a medicine depends heavily on one or a few non-EU countries, buyers must favour EU manufacturing through at least one of two mechanisms. One is reserving a lot covering at least 50% of the volume for suppliers offering the medicine and its active substance made in the EU. The other is scoring bids in proportion to the share made in the EU. Import, repackaging, labelling and quality testing do not count as manufacturing.
The line that price can no longer be the only criterion came from Parliament's rapporteur, Tomislav Sokol, and reflects Parliament's position of January 2026. The agreed text allows justified exceptions, for example when only one supplier can deliver or the cost would be disproportionate (Article 18(5)).

seccions.titol: What market it opens for equipment and service suppliers
seccions.text:
Article 18 tenders buy medicines, not bioreactors. Article 3 defines a supplier as the manufacturer or marketing authorisation holder of the finished product, or the manufacturer of active substances or key inputs. The Article 18 mechanisms reward where the medicine and its active substance are made, not where the equipment comes from. For equipment suppliers, the opportunity may come from customers investing to manufacture in the EU.
Which medicines are covered matters too. The EMA says the current Union list of critical medicines holds more than 200 active substances. A CDMO or a maker of reagents or primary packaging can fall within the Article 3 definition of supplier. Check whether your customers make anything on the list.

seccions.titol: Claims that do not hold up and what to say instead
seccions.text:
The biggest risk is treating the act as a seal of approval. It does not approve equipment or certify suppliers, and it is not law yet. One overstated claim makes quality and purchasing teams doubt the rest of your website, and the table suggests wording you can defend.
For a CDMO, Article 18 gives a useful hint. Where proof of EU manufacturing is required, it must come with documents the buyer can verify independently. Explaining which steps happen in the EU, in the same terms as the text, does more than any slogan in a CDMO's B2B marketing.

seccions.titol: How to cover it on your website, at trade shows and in meetings
seccions.text:
On your website, a short page about the act works better than a line on the home page. It should say where the act stands, what the articles relevant to your customers say and what you bring, with a date and a link to the Council, the Commission or Parliament.
At trade shows and customer meetings, lead with the customer's project. Ask whether they have a site that could qualify as a strategic project or whether they sell medicines on the list. Prepare data on capacity, efficiency or innovative processes without saying the act requires it. If you manufacture in the BioRegion of Catalonia, say where you build your equipment and where you provide service from.
If you sell bioprocess equipment, marketing for biotech and bioprocess companies should start from these details rather than the headline. At crida studio we work on the message for each member of the buying committee and the evidence behind it.

faqs.q: Is the Critical Medicines Act already law?
faqs.a: Not yet. The text was agreed on 12 May 2026 and Parliament's plenary vote is provisionally set for 23 November, ahead of Council adoption and publication in the Official Journal. Under Article 31, it will apply from the first publication in the Official Journal of the Union list of critical medicines.

faqs.q: Can a bioprocess equipment maker have a strategic project?
faqs.a: The text does not say so explicitly. Article 5 covers EU projects that create, expand or modernise manufacturing capacity, and point d includes projects that help roll out a technology key to manufacturing critical medicines. Whether a specific project qualifies is decided by the designated authority in each member state (Article 6).

faqs.q: Does the act affect how pharma companies buy equipment?
faqs.a: Not directly. The public procurement rules in Article 18 apply to public buyers of critical medicines. Any effect on equipment may come later, if pharma companies decide to manufacture more in the EU to win those tenders or to use the benefits of strategic projects.

bio-testimonis-usuaris-cientifics.intro: A testimonial from a scientist works when it carries a name, a job title and an institution, describes a specific application and gives, in their own words, the result they choose to share. Get their consent in writing and, if the university is named, ask the institution too. Any loaned equipment, discount, collaboration or fee belongs in a line next to the quote.

seccions.titol: What to ask for so the quote convinces another scientist
seccions.text:
A believable quote says who is speaking, what they do and what they achieved. “Very happy with the system” signed with a set of initials reads like an ad. A lab head with a name, a group and an institution, who explains what she uses the bioreactor for and at what scale, speaks the reader's language.
Do not write the quote for her. Have a short conversation with open questions, such as what problem she had or what has changed in the lab, and let her pick the result. Then send her the draft to correct and approve. These are the details worth collecting.

seccions.titol: Who needs to approve it besides the scientist
seccions.text:
The first approval comes from the person, in writing. It should say where the quote will appear and for how long, for example on the website, at trade shows or on LinkedIn. Ask her as well whether her institution has rules on using its name and logo, and who signs them off.
The US FTC guides on endorsements say in section 255.0(b) that the name or seal of an organisation can be an endorsement, and in section 255.4 that an organisation's endorsement must reflect its collective judgement. If only the researcher is speaking, make it clear the view is hers, just as with papers that cite your equipment.

seccions.titol: Loaned equipment, discounts or fees and what to disclose
seccions.text:
Section 255.5(a) of the FTC guides says that a connection between endorser and seller that might materially affect the weight or credibility of the endorsement, and that the audience would not reasonably expect, must be disclosed clearly and conspicuously. That covers payments, free or discounted products, even with no endorsement required in return, and early access.
The same section says a disclosure does not need the full details, but it must make the nature of the connection clear. One line under the quote can be enough, for example “The system was loaned to the lab for evaluation”. These are the usual cases in this sector.

seccions.titol: Where each testimonial goes on your website
seccions.text:
Each quote sits next to the decision it helps with. On the product page, beside the technical claim it confirms. On the application page, grouped by process and scale. And on the demo request landing page, close to the form.
When we build the website for an equipment maker, we store testimonials as records with the application, model, institution, approval date and declared connection. Each page then shows the ones that belong there, and when a consent expires the quote disappears from every page at once.

seccions.titol: Video or text, depending on what the institution can approve
seccions.text:
Text is easier to approve, translate and update. Video adds a face, a voice and the lab, but it needs more approvals, such as permission to film in a university lab. The shot can also include other brands' equipment or screens showing data.
If there is a connection to disclose, section 255.0(f) of the FTC guides says the disclosure should appear at least where the message is made, on screen, in the audio or in both. If the user wants to tell the whole project story, you have material for a full case study.

seccions.titol: Should testimonials get structured data markup?
seccions.text:
Usually not. Google's review snippet documentation requires an author and a rating for each marked-up review, and a quote has no rating. Google also says that when an entity controls the reviews about itself, its pages using Organization or LocalBusiness markup are not eligible for review stars.
The same page says not to include fake reviews, or reviews written in exchange for money, discounts or free products that do not clearly and prominently disclose it. Publish the testimonial as visible text, with the declared connection right below it.

seccions.titol: When to ask again and what the EU rules say
seccions.text:
Ask again when the model changes or the person moves to another job. Section 255.1(b) says an expert endorsement can only be used while there is good reason to believe the expert still holds those views, and lists a material change in the product among the factors for checking again.
In the EU, Directive (EU) 2019/2161 added Article 7(6) and points 23b and 23c of Annex I to Directive 2005/29/EC, which covers unfair business-to-consumer commercial practices. These new provisions deal with consumer reviews and endorsements.
Sorting out testimonials, approvals and the pages they appear on is part of our marketing for biotech, bioprocess and pharma companies, which we offer to equipment makers and CDMOs. We start by checking which quotes you already have approved in writing.

faqs.q: Can I put the university logo next to the quote?
faqs.a: Not without the institution's permission. Section 255.0(b) of the FTC guides says the name or seal of an organisation can be an endorsement, and a logo may suggest the university recommends your equipment. Without that permission, give the institution's name in plain text, below the person's name.

faqs.q: If a KOL is paid to give a webinar, do I have to say so when I use their opinion?
faqs.a: If the connection could affect the weight of the quote and the audience would not expect it, section 255.5(a) of the FTC guides says it must be disclosed, and payments are among its examples. You do not need the full details, only a clear statement of the connection, such as “Paid scientific adviser to the company”.

faqs.q: Can I shorten what the scientist said?
faqs.a: Yes, as long as the meaning stays the same. Section 255.1(b) says that if you use quotation marks, the words must be exactly the endorser's, and that an endorsement cannot be taken out of context or reworded in a way that distorts their opinion. Send them the shortened version to approve.

calculadora-pressupost-web.intro: This calculator adds up what your website, branding, 3D renders, video, automation and SEO or Google Ads would cost at the starting prices crida studio publishes. A simple website starts at €1,200, a custom website at €3,000 and a new brand at €3,500, all excluding VAT. Everything is calculated in your browser and nothing is sent anywhere.

seccions.titol: Work out the cost of your website and marketing
seccions.text:
Pick the website, the brand work and anything else you need, then add SEO or Google Ads if you also want to count what is paid every month. The calculator adds up the starting price of each service, keeps one-off work apart from monthly fees and gives you the total for the months you choose, first without VAT and then with Spanish VAT at 21 %.
The result is the starting price, the minimum each service costs without add-ons. The final figure depends on the number of pages and languages, who writes the copy and what the website has to connect to. The calculator does not store or send anything, and your selection is gone when you close the page.

seccions.titol: What each starting price includes
seccions.text:
A simple template website starts at €1,200 and has three to five pages in one language, with your own copy, a contact form, a map and an hour of training. A custom WordPress business website starts at €3,000 and has five to eight pages with an original design. If you are unsure whether a bespoke website or a template suits you, compare what each one gives you first.
An online shop starts at €4,000 with up to 50 products in one language, with payments and shipping set up. A new brand starts at €3,500 with a logo, colours, typography, a short brand guide and the basic applications. A rebrand starts at €4,000, and we do not design a logo on its own.
A product render on a neutral background starts at €250 per image for one view, and an interior of one room at €350. Both come with two rounds of revisions, and a pack of 3 to 5 images starts at €2,000. A 60 to 90 second explainer video with script, 2D animation and voice-over in one language starts at €2,500.
Automating one process across two or three tools starts at €1,200, with testing and documentation. Ona, our voice assistant for websites, costs €149 a month with a 12-month commitment, plus a €750 setup. Maintenance is included, and AI usage is billed separately based on use. The pricing page has the full card for each service, with what can be added to it.

seccions.titol: Why these are starting prices and what pushes them up
seccions.text:
They are starting prices because one five-page website can cost twice as much as another. Four things decide it. How many pages the site has, how many languages it needs, who writes the copy and what it has to connect to, such as a CRM, a booking system or an ERP.
Each service has published add-ons. A simple website can grow to eight pages or a second language, and a custom one to ten or twenty pages in three languages, with a blog or copy written by us. If the site needs bookings, private areas or an ERP connection, custom development starts at €8,000.
So before you compare offers, list what the website has to do and give every studio the same scope. When you compare web design proposals, look at what each price includes and not only at the final figure.

seccions.titol: What you pay every month and for how long
seccions.text:
Monthly SEO starts at €450 a month and covers local SEO, your Google Business Profile, your key pages and a monthly report. Plan on three to six months at the very least, which is why the calculator starts at 12 months. If your market is national or international, that SEO is quoted as an add-on.
Google Ads management starts at €790 a month and includes search campaigns, lead tracking and a monthly report. Ad spend is separate. You pay it to Google from your own account, before or after the ads run depending on how the account is set up, and it makes sense from €900 a month.
Two things Google says help with the sums. Advertising with Google has no effect on your site’s presence in the organic search results, so SEO and ads are separate budget lines. And for most campaigns, Google never charges more than 30.4 times your average daily budget in a month. Multiply your daily budget by 30.4 to get the monthly maximum.
Some costs come with any website, whoever builds it. Maintenance with updates, backups and monitoring runs from €40 to €120 a month depending on the website, a domain from €10 to €40 a year and hosting from €100 to €300 a year. The calculator leaves them out because they are paid separately and quoted as ranges.

seccions.titol: Three worked examples with the published prices
seccions.text:
A company launching a new brand and website. A new brand starts at €3,500 and a custom business website at €3,000. That makes €6,500 before VAT, €1,365 of Spanish VAT and €7,865 in total. The brand takes five to eight weeks, and the website six to ten weeks from when the copy and images are ready.
An online shop that wants to be found on Google. The shop starts at €4,000 and six months of SEO at €2,700. The first six months add up to €6,700 before VAT, or €8,107 with Spanish VAT. If the SEO carries on, each extra month adds €450. We used six months because SEO needs three to six months at the very least.
A business that wants enquiries straight away. A simple website starts at €1,200 and Google Ads management at €790 a month. Over 12 months that comes to €10,680 before VAT, or €12,922.80 with Spanish VAT. Ad spend comes on top and makes sense from €900 a month, so allow at least €10,800 a year paid to Google.

seccions.titol: How long it takes and how you get a fixed quote
seccions.text:
The usual timelines are published too. A simple website takes three to four weeks. A custom website takes six to ten weeks from when the copy and images are ready. A new brand takes five to eight weeks, and a render one to two weeks per image. Other timelines are set out in the proposal.
A fixed quote starts with a thirty-minute call with no commitment, where you tell us what you need. Within five working days you get a written proposal with the scope, the timeline and a fixed price. The work then runs in phases, and you see each phase before the next one starts.
When the work is finished, you get the website with full access. The first month after launch is included, and after that monthly maintenance is optional. The website is yours, with the domain, hosting and logins in your name and no lock-in.

seccions.titol: What you can do today before asking for a quote
seccions.text: These four steps will get you to the call with what it takes to fix the figure in a single conversation. You do not need to have everything decided, but you should know what is essential now and what can wait for a second phase.

faqs.q: Can I order just a logo?
faqs.a: No. We do not design a logo on its own, because the brand has to say what you do today. A new brand starts at €3,500 excluding VAT and includes a logo, colours, typography, a short brand guide and the basic applications. If you already have a brand and want to bring it up to date, a rebrand starts at €4,000.

faqs.q: Is the calculator’s figure the final price?
faqs.a: No. It is the sum of the starting prices, the minimum for each service without add-ons. The final price depends on the number of pages and languages, who writes the copy and what the website has to connect to. You get it in writing within five working days, after a thirty-minute call with no commitment.

faqs.q: How much should I budget for Google Ads?
faqs.a: There are two amounts. Management starts at €790 a month excluding VAT, and the ad spend is paid separately, straight to Google. It makes sense from €900 a month, because below that there is not enough data to improve the campaigns. Over a year that is at least €10,800 in ads and €9,480 in management.

faqs.q: Why does the calculator add 21 % VAT?
faqs.a: Because 21 % is the general VAT rate in Spain, under article 90 of Law 37/1992. All the prices exclude VAT, and the calculator shows it on a separate line. If your company is based outside Spain, or in the Canary Islands, Ceuta or Melilla, Spanish VAT may not apply, and the proposal states which tax it carries.

faqs.q: What does a website quote include? An example
faqs.a: A fixed quote says what will be done, how long it takes and what it costs, with VAT on top. With our starting prices, a simple website starts at €1,200, a bespoke corporate website at €3,000 and an online shop at €4,000, all excluding VAT. Above you have three complete examples with the first-year total.

faqs.q: Does the calculator store or send what I enter?
faqs.a: No. Everything is calculated in your browser by a small script, and nothing is sent to crida studio or anyone else. Your selection is not stored anywhere and disappears when you close or reload the page. If you want to keep the result, take a screenshot or note the figures before you leave.

bio-anticossos-monoclonals-autoritzats-e.intro: We counted 271 monoclonal antibody authorisations in the EMA's medicines file, from 1996 to 18 September 2026. 2025 set the record with 49, which is 45 % of the 109 medicines the EU authorised centrally that year. 34 of the 49 were biosimilars, most of them denosumab. New antibody substances come at a steadier pace, 13 in 2025, and they reach more diseases.

seccions.titol: How many monoclonal antibodies the EMA authorises each year
seccions.text:
The EMA's medicines file holds 271 monoclonal antibodies for human use with an EU marketing authorisation. The first two date from 1996. 231 are still authorised today, and the other 40 were withdrawn, revoked, expired or lapsed. Each brand name counts once, so one molecule sold under two brands counts twice.
From 1996 to 2014 the number stayed small, between zero and six a year. 2015 and 2016 brought 10 and 8, and the big jump came in 2017 and 2018, with 20 and 22, when the biosimilars of rituximab, adalimumab and trastuzumab arrived. 2021 also reached 22. Then came 30 in 2024 and 49 in 2025, the highest figure in the file.
2026 has 13 so far, with the latest authorisation dated 18 September, far below the 49 of 2025. Six more antibodies sit in the file with the status Opinion. Five have a positive EMA opinion and are waiting for the European Commission decision, and one has a negative opinion.

seccions.titol: Antibodies are now close to half of EU central approvals
seccions.text:
In 2025 the EU authorised 109 human medicines through the centralised procedure, and 49 of them were monoclonal antibodies. That is 45 %. In 2024 the share was 30 % and in 2019 it was 14 %. This counts all medicines in the file, including generics and biosimilars, by the date of their authorisation.
Over five-year periods the change is clearer. From 1996 to 2000 there were 10 antibodies out of 150 central authorisations, or 7 %. From 2021 to 2025 there were 133 out of 467, or 28 %. Medicines made by biotechnology must go through the EMA, so this file is the reference list for antibodies in the EU.

seccions.titol: Biosimilars drive the record, new antibodies keep a steady pace
seccions.text:
Of the 49 antibodies authorised in 2025, 34 are biosimilars. 26 are denosumab, the bone medicine, and 5 are ustekinumab. In 2024 the wave was ustekinumab, with 9 of the 17 biosimilar antibodies. The 26 denosumab biosimilars of 2025 belong to 14 different holders, and the 9 ustekinumab ones of 2024 to 7.
New antibody substances follow another rhythm. We counted an antibody as new the first time its name appears in the file. There were 13 in 2021, 14 in 2022, 9 in 2023, 10 in 2024 and 13 in 2025, for 59 in five years. From 2016 to 2020 there were 40, and from 2006 to 2015 there were 31.
For a supplier these are two different buyers. A biosimilar developer already knows the molecule and competes on cost and on time to market. A company with a new antibody is still scaling up, often with a CDMO. Our guide on EMA-approved biosimilars lists every molecule and holder. The EMA's own 2025 report mentions 41 biosimilars, but that covers every type of biosimilar and counts opinions, not authorisation dates.
The 231 antibodies authorised today belong to 88 holders. Roche Registration has 15, Amgen Europe 12, Celltrion 11, Sandoz 10 and Samsung Bioepis 9. All of the Celltrion, Sandoz and Samsung Bioepis ones are biosimilars, and none of Roche's are. The holder is not always the manufacturer, but it is the first name on an account list.

seccions.titol: Which diseases and formats the new antibodies target
seccions.text:
Cancer leads. Of the 59 new antibody substances from 2021 to 2025, 26 carry an ATC code for antineoplastic agents and 13 for immunosuppressants. Two more, for myeloma and lymphoma, had no ATC code yet in the file. The rest are spread wide, with 6 against COVID-19 and RSV, 3 for atopic dermatitis and 2 for haemophilia.
2025 brought lecanemab and donanemab, the first two antibodies for Alzheimer's disease in the file. It also brought garadacimab for hereditary angioedema and nemolizumab for prurigo. None of the four is a cancer drug, so the buyers of new antibodies are no longer only in oncology.
